fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Acacia: from the Greek 'akakia' and in turn from the Egyptian 'ake' meaning a point or thorn. 
The Australian Acacias don't have thorns.
cultriformis: from the Latin 'culter' (a knife) and 'formis' (in the form of) referring to the shape of the phyllodes.
fields.Description:
A shrub or small tree often with many stems from the base.
The seedlings have compound leaves but these are soon replaced by triangular phyllodes (winged leaf stalks that function as leaves).
fields.Notes:
Not a listed Invasive, but it is potentially a problem plant in our reserves.
CONTROL:  Cut the plants down to just above the ground and paint the stump immediately with Kaput.  Don't use excessive amounts of Kaput and be careful not to spill it or get it straight onto the soil.
If spraying is necessary for any reason TARGET SPRAY to avoid spraying other plants, using one of about 10 herbicides containing Triclopyr.  DO NOT SPRAY with a product containing Picloram. It is NOT appropriate in a nature area.
Indigenous to Australia.

Distinguishing features are:
- Silvery leaves
fields.Notes:

fields.Description:
A evergreen tree ± 8-20 metres tall depending on its location.
Distinguishing features are 
- Seedlings have compound leaves as usual.
- Within a few weeks the leaf stem of each new leaf is a partially formed phyllode (the winged leaf stalk that functions as a leaf) with a typical twice-compound leaves at its end.
- Finally the tree has no leaves, only long narrow phyllodes.
Pale yellow flowers.
fields.Notes:

podalyriifolia: leaf similar to that of Podalyria ( a South African plant)
fields.Description:

It is a small, evergreen tree up to ± 5 metres.
Distinguishing features are
- Only the seedlings have the usual compound leaves.  They are soon replaced by grey-green phyllodes.
- Yellow flowers.
- Large pods with swellings where the seeds are.
fields.Notes:

fields.Family: EUPHORBIACEAE, the Euphorbia or Poinsettia family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Acalypha: from the Ancient Greek for nettle.
brachiata: at right angles, arm-like
fields.Description:
Small perennial, ±400-500mm
Leaves ±100mm x ±20mm densely covered with hairs. 
Male and female inflorescences (the flower head) are generally on the same plant in mid-summer.  The male inflorescence is a spike in the axil of the leaves.  The female inflorescence is terminal (at the tip or apex of the stem).
Reddish leaves in the winter.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the Pretoria area.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape. 
Widespread in the drier parts of warm temperate to tropical Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Achyranthes: from the Greek 'αχυρων' (achyron) meaning straw, chaff or husk.
aspera: From the Latin 'aspera' meaning rough.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb, ±30-60 mm tall. 
Its leaves have short stalks, are dark green above and paler below, in opposite pairs ±40 x 25 mm, tapering to a point at both ends and densely to sparsely hairy.
The small, greenish-white flowers are on long, narrow spikes. As the flowers age, they bend downwards and become pressed closely against the stem. 
Bracts surrounding the fruits have sharp, pointed tips and are spiny to the touch. The sharp-pointed fruits are orange to reddish purple or straw-brown.
fields.Notes:
A troublesome WEED (declared invasive in several countries).
CONTROL: TARGET SPRAY with one of about 10 herbicides containing Triclopyr.  DO NOT SPRAY with a product containing Picloram. It is NOT appropriate in a nature area.
Its origin is unclear, possibly indigenous to south-east Asia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Achyropsis: uncertain.
leptostachya: 'leptos' Greek for thin, 'stakhys' spike of wheat.
fields.Description:
A small perennial subshrub, with quite woody older stems.
The opposite, grey-green leaves have very short leaf stems, are long and narrow.
The Inflorescence is a slender spike on a tall stem. 
The tiny (±1 mm) flower buds are green, close-set, and held between green bracts.  As they start to open they show some white.  
The rounded flowers open only slightly and are green with yellow stamens. 
The fruits are subglobose (not quite spherical and are still nestled between the bracts).
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.
Also in tropical Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Afrocanthium: an African genus close to Canthium.
mundianum: presumably after someone called Mundt
fields.Description:
An upright shrub or small tree with greyish-brown main stem and branches.  The lateral branches are angled slightly upward.
The bright green leaves are hairless, slightly glossy, in pairs and they have a short petiole (leaf stem).
In early summer the tree has clusters of 3mm pale greenish yellow flowers with 5 petals. 
The fruit is more or less round but flattened and with a deep indent at the apex.
The leaves turn dark yellow in autumn.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.
Also in tropical Africa.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, and parts of KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern and Western Cape.  Also native to Zimbabwe and Mozambique.

fields.Family: ASPARAGACEAE, the Asparagus family, AGAVOIDEAE, the Agave subfamily
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Agave: from the Greek ‘agauos’ (admirable), referring to the very tall inflorescences. 
americana: ‘of America’, referring to its American origin.
fields.Description:
An evergreen perennial with huge succulent leaves arranged in a rosette.  
The GREY-GREEN leaves are long (±2 metres x 150-250 mm), thickened, and carried on a short stem that is thickened by the prominent leaf bases. The leaf margins are nearly straight and armed with teeth of up to 10 mm long and 10–40 mm apart. 
After some years the plant produces a thick flowering stem ±3-4 metres tall.  After flowering and setting seed the plant dies and it produces several suckers that can be some distance from the original plant.
fields.Notes:
A Category 3 invasive in the Western Cape but not listed in Gauteng.  Nevertheless it is NOT appropriate in a Gauteng nature reserve.
CONTROL: TARGET SPRAY with one of about 10 herbicides containing Triclopyr.  DO NOT SPRAY with a product containing Picloram. It is NOT appropriate in a nature area.
It is indigenous to Mexico and the southern states of the United States.

fields.Family: ASPARAGACEAE, the Asparagus family, AGAVOIDEAE, the Agave subfamily
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Agave: from the Greek ‘agauos’ (admirable), referring to the very tall inflorescences.
fields.Description:
An evergreen perennial with succulent leaves arranged in a rosette.
The GREY-GREEN leaves are up to 1 metre long and thickened and have widely-spaced thorns on the margins and spiny, reddish-brown tips.
The flower spike is thick (±80 mm) and tall (±3 metres), the flowers are greenish-yellow.
Seeds are produced in an egg-shaped capsule and the plant produces plantlets that will grow when they drop to the ground.
fields.Notes:
A SERIOUS Category 2 INVASIVE.
CONTROL: TARGET SPRAY with one of about 10 herbicides containing Triclopyr.  DO NOT SPRAY with a product containing Picloram. It is NOT appropriate in a nature area.
It is native to southern Mexico.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ageratina: the suffix 'ina' suggests that Ageratina is related to Ageratum. 
adenophora: from the Greek 'aden' (a gland), and 'phoros' (bearing) referring to the oil-producing glands in the leaves.
fields.Description:
A perennial subshrub ±500 mm tall (that grows taller in favourable positions). 
The leaves are in opposite pairs ± 60 mm x 30 mm. 
The small ±5 mm compound flowers appear in clusters at the end of branches in late spring and summer. 
They are followed by a small brown seed with a white feathery 'parachute'.
fields.Notes:
A SERIOUS Category 1b INVASIVE.  It is more or less under control in Kruin Park.
CONTROL: TARGET SPRAY with one of about 10 herbicides containing Triclopyr.  DO NOT SPRAY with a product containing Picloram. It is NOT appropriate in a nature area.
It is native to Mexico and Central America.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Albuca: white.
glauca: from Ancient Greek, 'Gla͂ukos' (silvery, greyish or bluish.)
fields.Description:
Deciduous bulbous perennial.
The flower spike appears before the leaves in early spring. Green and yellowish flowers follow.
Leaves bluish green.  
The fruit is a green capsule that splits at the end and the seeds disperse as the capsule turns papery and light brown. Often grows in shade or partial shade.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.
Also in tropical Africa.
Occurs in Gauteng and Mpumalanga. Also found beyond the borders of South Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Aloe: from the Greek word 'alsos' (bitter sap).
arborescens: Tree-like.
fields.Description:
A 2-3 metre shrub with many branches.
It forms rosettes of ±20 grey green leaves with no spots. The leaf margins are armed with conspicuous pale teeth.
The ± 120-150 mm tapering flower spikes appear in winter.  They are usually orange to reddish-orange.
fields.Notes:
NOT native to the Pretoria area.
Indigenous to the eastern parts of South Africa from Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape to the Cape Peninsula.
Also native to Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Malawi.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Aloe: from the Greek word 'alsos' (referring to its bitter sap).
davyana: to honour Joseph Burtt Davy, who was the Director of the Divgision of Botany when it was established.
fields.Description:
A stemless Aloe that grows singly or in groups. The succulent leaves are arranged in a basal rosette. The leaves are striped above with oblong whitish spots arranged in more or less distinct bands; the leaf margins are armed with sharp, dark brown teeth. In winter, the tips of the leaves dry and become brown and twisted.
Aloe davyana flowers in winter. The inflorescence (i.e. the flower spike) is generally less than 1 metre high and has several branches. More than one inflorescence may be produced on one plant. The flowers are mostly pale pink.  An orange form and a darker pale reddish form occurs in Kruin Park
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.
Also in tropical Africa. 
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Free State.
Also occurs in Swaziland

fields.Common Names: Highveld Spotted aloe (Eng.); Transvaalaalwyn, grasaalwyn (Afr.); Kgopane (Setsswana)
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Aloe: from the Greek word 'alsos' (referring to its bitter sap).
davyana: to honour Joseph Burtt Davy, who was the Director of the Divgision of Botany when it was established.
fields.Description:
A stemless Aloe that grows singly or in groups. The succulent leaves are arranged in a basal rosette. The leaves are striped above with oblong whitish spots arranged in more or less distinct bands; the leaf margins are armed with sharp, dark brown teeth. In winter, the tips of the leaves dry and become brown and twisted.

Orange and a darker pale reddish forms occur in Kruin Park
fields.Notes: INTRODUCED to some reserves in Pretoria.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Aloe: from the Greek word 'alsos' (bitter sap).
fosteri: named after Mr Cyril Foster.
fields.Description:
The plants in Kruin Park are not true Aloe fosteri, they are hybrids.  The following description is for the species that occurs in the wild.
Growing in its natural habitat, Aloe fosteri is stemless and it forms a rosette on the ground.
Its leaves are spotted with H-shaped spots (the spots are NOT H-shaped in Kruin Park). They are dark green in summer and they tend to become reddish with dry tips in the winter.  The edges of the leaves have teeth.
The inflorescence (flower stem) is tall (± 1 metre) and with many branches.  The flowers range from yellow to orange and red.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to Kruin Park and tending to invade the Quartzite area of the reserve. So it should be kept to a small area.
It is not at risk of hybridising with the winter flowering Aloe davyana.
Indigenous to a very restricted part of the Limpopo and Mpumalanga Highveld west of the escarpment between Lydenburg and Polokwane.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Aloe: from the Greek word 'alsos' (bitter sap).
globuligemma: from the Latin ‘globulus’ (little ball) and ‘gemma’ (bud), a reference to the globular flower buds.
fields.Description:
A more or less stemless Aloe, that spreads to form dense clumps.
Each plant has up to 20 grey-green quite upright leaves that can be pinkish-grey-green in dry weather.  They are ± 300-450 mm long and ± 60-80 mm wide and they have widely spaced, ±2 mm long, off-white teeth.
One or two upright, ±600-1000 mm tall flower stems appear on the plants in early winter.  They have 3-8 quite horizontal branches.  The globular flower buds are closely placed on the upper side of these branches, they are dull red and paler at the top and the open flowers are mainly ivory to yellowish.
fields.Notes:
NOT native to the Pretoria area.
Indigenous to Limpopo and Mpumalanga and Limpopo Province.  Common from the Lydenburg district to Sekhukhuneland and the Olifants River Valley, and abundant along the Limpopo River and the northern side of the Soutpansberg.
Also indigenous to Zimbabwe and Botswana.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Aloe: from the Greek word 'alsos', (bitter sap).
marlothii: after the well-known botanist H.W. Rudolf Marloth.
fields.Description:
A tall, single-stemmed tree Aloe, up to 2 metres in Kruin Park, up to 6 metres elsewhere.  
The leaves are alternate, fleshy succulent and dull green to bluish green, armed with thorns.  Old leaves are brown and remain on the plant.  
The tubular flowers are orange with protruding stamens, and they point upwards and away from the tip of the inflorescence (the flower head).  
The fruits are green tinged with red and turn brown when they dry and ready to release the seeds.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.
Also in tropical Africa.
Widespread in the bushveld areas of Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, and northern KwaZulu-Natal.  
Also in Swaziland and Mozambique

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Aloe: from the Greek word 'alsos', (bitter sap).
pretoriensis: from Pretoria.
fields.Description:
A stemless Aloe with a rosette of leaves quite close to the ground.
The leaves are ±200-250mm x 40-60mm wide, succulent, greyish green with no spots, margins are armed with thorny teeth.
The flower stem forms about 5 branches at about 1 metre high, the flower heads are long and conical and the tubular flowers are pinkish red.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.
Also in tropical Africa.
ORIGINALLY Native to Kruin Park, but the one plant disappeared, presumably stolen.
Occurs in Limpopo, Gauteng and Mpumalanga (threatened in Gauteng due to habitat loss)
Also occurs in Swaziland and eastern Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Aloe: from the Greek word 'alsos' (bitter sap).
fields.Description:
A tall, single-stemmed tree Aloe, up to 2 metres in Kruin Park.
The leaves are alternate, fleshy succulent and dull green to bluish green, armed with thorns on the margins of the leaves.  Old leaves are brown and remain on the plant.  
The individual flower spikes are cylindrical resembling a bottle bush.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to northern KwaZulu-Natal, Swaziland and southern Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Aloe: from the Greek word 'alsos' (bitter sap).
wickensii: named to honour for John Edward Wickens a British-born horticulturist and plant collector who came to South Africa in 1888.
fields.Description:
This Aloe is usually stemless and it grows alone or in small groups. 
The leaves are ±500-700 x 100 mm, in an upright rosette. They are dull greyish-green to olive green, with no spines on the surface.  The leaf margins have small reddish brown teeth.
The flower stems appear in winter and they are upright, ±700-800 mm tall and branched.  The flowers are in a short cone with the oldest at the base and the youngest at the top.  The buds are reddish turning yellow as the flower opens.
fields.Notes:
Some sources refer to Aloe wickensii as Aloe cryptopoda or Aloe cryptopoda var wickensii 
INTRODUCED to some reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo and Mpumalanga (Aloe cryptopoda has a wider distribution and some sources suggest that A. wickensii is also native to North West and Gauteng).
Also native to Swaziland, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Alternanthera: means alternating anthers, referring to the arrangement of fertile stamens next to infertile ones in the flower. pungens: from the Latin word 'to prick' and refers to the prickly seed head.
fields.Description: A prostrate, creeping perennial plant with shiny oval leaves.  Clusters of small white flowers form in the leaf axils.  The papery fruits are stemless, ±6-9 mm, khaki-coloured, and prickly and they attach to the soles of our shoes and to animals feet.
fields.Notes:
A TROUBLESOME WEED because its seeds attach to shoes and clothing and to the feet and fur of animals.
The plant is a pest wherever it grows, and it has become a noxious weed in many countries. It has become widely established on roadsides, path verges and neglected land in South Africa. 
CONTROL: It is easy to control this plant with the most basic herbicides but because they are small and insignificant the trick is to find the plants.
It is thought to have come from Central and South America.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ancylobothrys: from the Greek 'ancylo' - crooked or bent and 'botrys' - cluster or bunch.
capensis:  southern Africa (literally from the Cape).
fields.Description:
An evergreen shrub with scrambling or trailing branches.
Darkish green leaves with paler undersides and prominent veins. 
The flowers are white with a reddish corolla tube, and are sweetly scented.
The fruit is velvety, more or less globose (spherical) and pinkish orange.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
It is found on quartzite ridges in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Anredera: The name is thought to be derived from the Spanish word, enredadera (creeping or climbing plant).
cordifolia: heart-shaped leaves.
fields.Description:
An evergreen climber. 
It has heart-shaped, fleshy, bright green, shiny leaves ±40–100 mm long. 
Wart-like tubers are produced on the stems of the plant. They drop off very easily, root and grow into new plants.
It produces masses of small, creamy-white flowers on long flower stems of ±120-250 mm in length.
fields.Notes:
A SERIOUS Category 1b INVASIVE. it tends to regrow from the roots and young plants grow from tubers that drop to the ground.
CONTROL: Simply cutting the plants down is NOT appropriate because the tubers will drop onto the ground and grow. 
If the plant has grown into trees, obviously one can't spray into the air.  In this case, cut the plant down taking care to remove as many of the tubers as possible. Then TARGET spray with a herbicide that contains Triclopyr, taking care to avoid spraying other plants.  
WATCH THE AREA FOR REGROWTH OF YOUNG PLANTS.
In the root zone of precious plants one could TARGET spray with Glyphosate.
DO NOT SPRAY with a product containing Picloram. It is NOT appropriate in a nature area.
The plant is indigenous to South America.

fields.Family: AIZOACEAE, the Mesem or Vygie family.
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Aptenia: from the Greek 'apten' (wingless) referring to the wingless seed.
fields.Description:
An evergreen and fast-growing prostrate, succulent perennial, ±150 mm high.
The stems can be four-angled or rounded. 
The leaves are fleshy, flat, usually heart-shaped, ±60 x 25 mm, and are widely spaced usually in pairs. Bladder or water cells are scattered on the leaf surface and they shine in the sunlight. 
The flowers open during the day from spring to autumn and they close at night.  They are purple to red, shiny, ±10-15 mm wide and they are borne singly or in clusters on short flower stalks. 
The flowers are self-fertilised and the fruit is a capsule with four chambers.
fields.Notes:
NOT native to Gauteng.
Indigenous to Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.
It does not seem to be invasive but it should not be in our reserves.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Araujia: named after António de Araújo e Azevedo, a Portugese author and amateur botanist.
sericifera: from the Latin meaning "silk-bearing"
fields.Description:
A creeping or climbing vine that can climb up to ±4 or 5–7 metres high. It has a milky, smelly exudate. 
Its leaves are in opposite pairs, glossy and quite fleshy, ±70-100 mm x 35-50 mm, with entire (untoothed) margins.
The flowers, are cream-coloured and sometimes pinkish, chalice-shaped, ±15-20 mm across and appear in summer.
The fruits are pear-shaped fruits and ±70-100 mm long. They contain numerous black seeds attached to silky hairs that enable them to be dispersed by the wind.
fields.Notes:
A SERIOUS Category 1b INVASIVE.
CONTROL: Young plants are easily pulled out after rain.  Older plants should be cut a few centimetres above the ground and the cut should be painted with Kaput, taking care not to get the Kaput on the ground.  
Indigenous to South America.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Arctotis arctotoides: from the Greek 'arktos', (a bear) and 'otis', (an ear).
fields.Description:
A perennial groundcover that forms mats. 
The deeply lobed leaves are bright green above with whitish felt underneath and they have prominent midribs.
The inflorescence (flower head) has yellow ray florets (outer "petals")  and yellow disk florets.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Northern Cape, Eastern Cape and Western Cape

fields.Common Names: Pale Mexican Prickly Poppy, Witblom Bloudissel.
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Argemone: apparently from the Greek 'αργεμωνη' a name given by Dioscorides to a poppy-like plant.
fields.Description:
A very spiny annual herb growing up to ±700 mm high.  Cut stems release a yellow sap when cut. 
The spiny leaves are bluish-green with prominent white veins. 
Pale yellow flowers appear from September to January. 
The fruit is a spiny, grey-green capsule.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE.
CONTROL: Not a serious problem in Kruin Park. Easily controlled by target spraying individual plants.
Its exact native range is disputed but it is probably native to tropical America.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Arundo: from the Latin 'arundo' (a reed).
donax:
fields.Description:
A tall reed ±3 metres tall in Kruin Park but taller in moist conditions.  The hollow stems are ±20-30 mm in diameter. 
The grey-green sword-like leaves are alternate, ±300-600 mm long and ±20-40 mm wide tapering to a point.
It flowers in late summer, bearing whitish to purplish brown feathery plumes ±400-600 mm long.  It does not flower in Kruin Park.
It reproduces its tough, fibrous underground rhizomes that form knotty, spreading mats.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE.
CONTROL: Because it is a monocotyledon (commonly referred to as monocot) it cannot be controlled with the usually selective herbicides. TARGET spray with Glyphosate.
Indigenous to countries on the Mediterranean and to the Middle East.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Asparagus: from the Greek and originally from the Persian asparag, meaning "sprout" or "shoot".
flavicaulis: flavi, meaning yellow, caulis, meaning stem.
fields.Description:
A small sub-shrub up to 700mm with a perennial rootstock, it has spiny branches.
Leafless, it has cylindrical needle-like cladodes (stems that perform the function of leaves).
Six-petalled white flowers in spring.
The globose (spherical) fruit is a berry (with the seeds immersed in the pulp like a tomato).  Initially it is dark green, turning black or reddish.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.  Also found in Botswana and Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Asparagus: from the Greek and originally from the Persian asparag, meaning "sprout" or "shoot".
suaveolens: meaning 'sweet scented'.
fields.Description:
An erect sub-shrub up to ±1 m high.
The stems are erect, usually straight sometimes slightly zigzag, with numerous spines, branches and branchlets.
The “leaf” is a cladode (a leaf-like branch or stem that photosynthesises) in bundles, green, narrow and tapering to a point, ±10-19 mm long.
The flowers appear in December. They are whitish with a dark midrib, ±3-6 mm across.  The ovary is egg-shaped, 3-grooved, and yellowish.
The fruit is a black berry (i.e. like a tomato), ±5 mm in diameter, the dry perianth is persistent, 1–3-seeded.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Common in all of South Africa, it also occurs in southern Zimbabwe, parts of Namibia, Botswana, southern Mozambique and again in Malawi and in Kenya.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Asparagus: from the Greek and originally from the Persian 'asparag' - sprout or shoot.
virgatus: from the Latin 'virga' - twig or stalk, in reference to the way the leaves cluster at the top of the stems.
fields.Description:
Growing in shade it is a wispy evergreen herb, 400-600 mm high. 
The arching stems are branched and carry soft, thread-like "leaves" that are actually cladodes, about 10-12 mm long.
The flowers are inconspicuous and greenish white with recurved tepals, and they appear in summer.  They are followed by green, 5 mm fruits hanging on thin stems.  They turn red by late summer.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in all of South Africa except Western Cape.  It is found as far north as Angola and Tanzania.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Athrixia: possibly from the word thrix, referring to its hairy stems and leaves.
elata: generally means tall, its use here is unclear.
fields.Description:
A slender sub-shrub ±400mm x 600mm.
The leaves are ±15mm x 3mm with a sharp point and with recurved edges.  They are green but greyish underneath.  
The flowers are typical daisies pink to mauve and ±15mm across.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and northern Free State.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Barleria: named after the French monk and botanist, Jacques Barrelier.
obtusa: meaning blunt or rounded.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb that grows to ±500 mm high with the stems becoming woody.  
Its stems and leaves are hairy.
The leaves are oval ±50x30 mm and with very short leaf stalks.
The flowers are tubular opening up into 5 lobes, mauve or violet blue and with dark and pale veins in the throat.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Pretoria (Flora capensis (pp52-53) records that the Polish botanist, Anton Rehmann, gathered two specimens of Barleria obtusa from “Apies Poort, near Pretoria”.
INTRODUCED to other reserves in Pretoria and tending to invade the habitat of Barleria pretoriensis.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Barleria: named after the French monk and botanist, Jacques Barrelier.
pretoriensis: from Pretoria
fields.Description:
A low spreading sub-shrub, ±300-400mm high.
The leaves are ±250mm x 5mm, greyish-green.
The flowers are ±25-50mm long and as wide.  They are white but turn mauve with age.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.
Also in tropical Africa.
Indigenous to parts of Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.  Also beyond our borders.

fields.Common Names: Pride of De Kaap, Kameelpoot, Vlam-van-die-Vlakte
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Bauhinia: named by Linnaeus after the Bauhin brothers Gaspard and Jean, Swiss botanists of Huguenot parents.
galpinii: in honour of Ernest Galpin, a famous South African amateur botanist and plant collector.
fields.Description:
A medium to large shrub that will climb into trees.
The leaves are two-lobed, with quite prominent pale veins.
The terracotta red flowers appear from summer to autumn.
The fruit is a large pod.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to Pretoria's nature areas.
Indigenous to the moist bushveld of Limpopo, Mpumalanga, and northern Kwazulu-Natal.
Also indigenous to eastern Zimbabwe, Swaziland, and Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Bauhinia: named by Linnaeus to honour the Bauhin brothers Gaspard and Jean, Swiss botanists.
variegata: a reference to variegated colour of the middle petal.
fields.Description:
A deciduous, small to medium-sized tree usually up to ±5 or 6 metres tall.
The leaves are ±100-200 mm two-lobed and with quite conspicuous pale veins. 
The flowers are showy, usually bright pink but ALSO White, ±60-90 mm across, and they have five petals.
The fruit is a pod ±120-160 long, containing several seeds. It dries on the tree, and when the seeds are mature it twists before it explodes open and sends the seeds into the surrounding area.
fields.Notes:
A Category 3 INVASIVE in Gauteng.  
CONTROL: Cut larger plants down to just above the ground and paint the stump immediately with Kaput. Don't use excessive amounts of Kaput and be careful not to spill it or get it straight onto the soil.
TARGET SPRAY small plants to avoid spraying other plants, using herbicides containing Triclopyr, or a combination of Fluroxypyr and Triclopyr.
A product containing Picloram is NOT appropriate in a nature area because it persists in the soil and is translocated to other surrounding plants.
ORIGIN: Indigenous to south-east Asia from China to India.

fields.Scientific Name: Berchemia zeyheri, previously Phyllogeiton zeyheri and before that Rhamnus zeyheri
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Berchemia: in honour of the French botanist, M. Berchem
zeyheri: in honour of K.L.P. Zeyher, a German botanist who was active in South Africa in the early 19th century.
fields.Description:
A fine tree with a spreading crown up to 8 metres high.
The oval leaves have short petioles (leaf stems) and the veins are prominent.
The small flowers are carried in the axils of the leaves and are followed by red berries.
The leaves turn golden brown in autumn.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, northern Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.  Also found in Zimbabwe and Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Berkheya: named in honour of the Dutch scientist and artist Johannes le Francq van Berkhey.
radula: from the Latin ‘radere’ to scrape
fields.Description:
A prickly perennial herb, ±500mm to 1 metre tall. 
Its leaves are mostly close to the ground, green and rough textured above and pale felty below. The leaf margins have coarse teeth with spines on the tips of the teeth and smaller spines in between.
The flower stems are covered in spiny wings.
The flower bud is spiny and the open “flower” is a typical double daisy with yellow ray florets and darker disk florets.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Pretoria's wetland reserves.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, Free State and Eastern Cape.

fields.Common Names: Blackjack, Knapsekêrel, Mashola a Mugabe (Sepedi for Mugabe’s soldiers)
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Bidens: from the Latin 'bi’ and “dens' (two teeth) referring to the barbs on the seeds.
pilosa: covered with fine soft hairs.
fields.Description:
A slender herbaceous annual, up to 1 metres tall. 
The leaves are in opposite pairs, with three to five toothed leaflets of ±15-30 x 8-15 mm. 
It flowers in summer and autumn. The flower heads are typical daisies with four or five broad white ray florets while the disk florets are yellow.
The seeds are stiff and black, ±10mm long, with stiff, heavily barbed bristles at the ends that hook onto clothing or the fur of animals.
fields.Notes:
A troublesome WEED that grows aggressively on disturbed land. 
In terms of the Weeds Act of 1937, the Blackjack was a declared noxious weed. The Weeds Act was repealed in 1963 and the Blackjack is no longer a listed invasive.
We have controlled the worst of it in Kruin Park by pulling out the young plants along the paths before they set seed. 
Indigenous to the Americas.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Bolusanthus: in honour of Harry Bolus, a South African businessman and amateur botanist, whose bequeathed his personal herbarium to the South African College in Cape Town and who left a generous fund to extend and maintain the collection. 
speciosus: from the Latin meaning beautiful.
fields.Description:
A small to medium-sized deciduous tree that keeps its leaves through part of the winter. The bark is brownish grey and deeply fissured. 
Its leaves are pinnately compound (i.e. its leaflets are arranged on each side of a common leaf stem) with four to seven pairs of leaflets and a terminal leaflet.
The flowers are pea-like, bluish mauve and sweet-smelling and they appear in spring. They are followed by papery, brown fruit pods.
fields.Notes:
UNCERTAIN, probably introduced to reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, parts of Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.
Also native to Lesotho. Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Swaziland and Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Boophone: from the Greek 'bous' (ox), and 'phone' (death).
disticha: from the Latin meaning "2-ranked", referring to the leaf arrangement.
fields.Description:
A deciduous bulbous plant with dry scales above the ground, it flowers in spring and early summer before the leaves develop. 
The +- 300 mm wide flower head is on a short scape (stalk) and it has long individual flower stems that are all based at the top of the scape.
The pink to dark red flowers have 3 outer petals and 3 inner petals, and the long red stamens are tipped with white anthers.
The upright, greyish-green leaves are arranged in a conspicuous fan and are usually produced after flowering.  
The pedicels (flower stalks) elongate after flowering to form a large seed head that breaks off at the top of the scape (stalk) and tumbles across the veld, dispersing the seed.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to grassland reserves in Pretoria.
A grassland species, it occurs in all of South Africa and further north to tropical Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Brachylaena: from the Greek 'brachus', (short) and 'klaina', (cloak), referring to the short floral bracts.
fields.Description:
A deciduous tree of ±3-6 metres.
The young stems are greyish turning dark brown later.
The leaves are distinctive, greyish-green but much lighter grey-white underneath.
The tree is dioecious (male and female flowers occur on separate trees).
The flowers are ±3-4mm and yellowish-green.
The seed head consists of many seeds, each with a  stiff hair-like structure, called a pappus, attached to the top. The seed is parachute-like and is carried by the wind.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and Free State.  Also occurs in eastern Botswana, Mozambique, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Brassica: Uncertain meaning, various meanings have been suggested
fields.Description: A small annual herb with four-petalled yellow flowers.
fields.Notes: A WEED in some reserves in Pretoria.

fields.Common Names: Chandelier Plant, Mother of Millions, Kandelaarplant
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Bryophyllum: From the Greek ‘bryo’ (to sprout) and ‘phyllon’ (leaf) referring to the leaves that produce plantlets around their edges
delagoense: Maputo Bay was formerly known as Delagoa Bay from Baía da Lagoa in Portuguese.  The reference to the mainland for a plant indigenous to Madagascar is unclear.
fields.Description:
A succulent perennial with unbranched, upright stems.  It grows to a height of ±300-500 mm.
The stems are hairless and dark grey.
The leaves are fleshy, almost cylindrical ±75-150 mm long and 2-6 mm thick and they have a few small ‘teeth’ at the tips.  The leaves are grey with darker grey mottling.  Tiny plantlets develop among the teeth at the tips of the leaves that drop off and grow.
The outer calyx is greyish and has four partially joined sepals. The flowers are drooping, bell-shaped, ±15-30 mm long and orange-red. 
The dry, papery fruit is a follicle (splitting along a single suture, to which the seeds are attached) that remains hidden by the old calyx and it is ±8-10 mm long.
fields.Notes:
A potentially serious Category 1b INVASIVE.  It is very poisonous to livestock and humans and almost certainly also to wildlife.
We have controlled it in Kruin Park by target spraying the plants with Triclon and by watching for any young plants that reappear and spraying them.
Indigenous to Madagascar.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Burkea: in honour of Joseph Burke, the botanist and plant collector
africana: from Africa
fields.Description:
A fine deciduous tree up to 8 metres. 
It has attractive, bipinnately compound leaves that are ±100-250mm long, with 2-4 pairs of pinnae (secondary "stems") usually with ±10 or more greyish-green leaflets per pinna.  
The velvety brown tips to the branches are clearly visible in winter and early spring.
It has drooping flower stems in October with small pale greenish-yellow flowers.
The fruit is a grey woody pod.
Gold leaves in winter.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.  Also beyond our borders.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Campuloclinium: derivation uncertain. macrocephalum: large head.
fields.Description:
Perennial herb up to 600 mm high. 
The flower heads are terminal (carried at the ends of the branches) and the flowers appear from mid-summer to autumn.
The seed head consists of many seeds, each with a  stiff hair-like structure, called a pappus, attached to the top that results in the seed being dispersed widely by the wind.
fields.Notes:
A SERIOUS Category 1b INVASIVE, it threatens the survival of grasslands and wetlands in South Africa.
CONTROL:  A product containing Picloram is NOT appropriate in a nature area because it persists in the soil and is translocated to other surrounding plants.
TARGET SPRAY to avoid spraying other plants, using herbicides containing Triclopyr, Metsulfuron Methyl, or a combination of Fluroxypyr and Triclopyr.
Remove flower heads to prevent seed formation.
Native to Argentina, Brazil, Central America and Mexico.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Canthium: from 'canti', the Malabar (Indian) name for a plant in this genus
gilfillanii: after D. F. Gilfillan who collected the type specimen.
fields.Description:
A small deciduous tree of 2-4 metres.  It forms thickets that can become impenetrable.
The bark is grey and quite smooth.
The tiny, ±2-3mm flowers appear in late Spring and are yellowish-green.
The leaves are green and velvety.
The fruits are green turning black as they ripen.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Carissa: from the Indian name for plants of this genus.
bispinosa: from the Latin word, two-spined.
fields.Description:
A variable species, it can be a dense or a rambling shrub. It is evergreen and twiggy, the branches exhibiting a repeated forked pattern. The branches are often hairy.
The leaves and thorns show marked variation throughout its range. The leaves are in opposite pairs, dark green above, paler below, with a smooth margin.
The small white flowers appear in small clusters in March.  They have a slender corolla tube and five petals.
The fruit is a small, roundish, red berry (like a tomato).
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in wooded areas in Limpopo, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, eastern Free State, Eastern Cape and Western Cape.
Also occurs in Namibia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and sporadically further north as far as Kenya.

fields.Common Names: Natal plum, Num-num, Groot noem-noem, Amatungulu (Zulu)
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Carissa: from the Sanskrit corissa, the name of one of the Indian species.
macrocarpa: ‘macro’ meaning big, and ‘carpa’ fruit
fields.Description:
A dense, thorny, evergreen, shrub up to 3 or 4 metres in its natural habitat.  In the shallow soils of Kruin Park it smaller, from ±1-2 m high and only leafy after good rains.
The stems are green, straight or slightly zigzag.
The leaves are leathery, a shiny dark green above and paler below, 20-40 x 15-30 mm, egg-shaped, oval or almost round. The rounded tips of the leaves usually have a small, thorn-like point.
The white flowers appear in spring and early summer.  They vary from ±20-35 mm in diameter, and the inside of the flower tube is hairy.
The fruit is large, ±20 x 12 mm, red and egg-shaped.
fields.Notes:
NOT indigenous to the Pretoria area.
It grows mainly in coastal areas, usually on sand dunes and on the edges of coastal forests of Kwazulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.
Also indigenous to Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Casuarina: from the Indonesian ‘Kasuari’ (Cassowary) because of the “similarity” of the foliage to the Cassowary bird.
cunninghamiana: in honour of Allan Cunningham, an early Australian botanist.
fields.Description:
An evergreen tree up to ±20-35 m tall. 
New growth consists of permanent branchlets that eventually form the main stem and branches of the tree, and non-permanent (deciduous) branchlets that fall from the tree after 1-2 years of growth. 
The branchlets are needle-like and they consist of jointed segments, each with a series of ridges that photosynthesise like the leaves of other plants.  Each ridge ends in a small triangular tooth, which is the tip of a reduced leaf.  Collectively these teeth form a whorl of leaf tips at the apex of each segment. 
Adult trees have separate male and female flowers.  Male flowers appear at the tips of new deciduous branchlets, they are ±4-30 mm long and are arranged in whorls.
Small reddish female flowers appear in clusters of about 50 from the leaf axils on the permanent branchlets. 
The individual fruit is winged, known as a samara.  It is single-seeded, pale greyish-yellow and ±3-4 mm long.
fields.Notes:
A Category 2 INVASIVE but Category 1b within 100 metres of “untransformed land” (such as a nature reserve) or a wetland or river. It has been troublesome in Kruin Park. 
Indigenous and endemic to Australia, it is still grown here as an ornamental tree.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Catharanthus: Uncertain, ‘anthus’ usually refers to the flower.
roseus: meaning rosy or pink.
fields.Description:
A perennial sub-shrub (somewhat woody at the base), usually upright, 300-600 mm high.
Its stems are green or dark red, ridged and often covered with short, soft, downy hairs.
Its leaves are green with paler veins, in opposite pairs, 25-70 mm long, more or less egg-shaped, with a tiny point extending from the main vein.
Its flowers are borne in the leaf axils, either singly or in pairs.
It has five short sepals (the outer whorl of the flower that is usually green). Its petals are fused at the base into a long narrow tube and it has five lobes.  They are usually pink but sometimes white.
The fruit is a follicle (pod-like but splitting along only one side) 20-35 mm long.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE.  It is a common garden plant in South Africa that frequently escapes to inhabit roadsides, abandoned quarries and farmland.
Indigenous and endemic to Madagascar

fields.Family: CANNABACEAE, the Cannabis or Hemp family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Celtis: the name used by Pliny, the Roman author and naturalist
africana: from Africa
fields.Description:
In a forest habitat such as in Fountains Valley it grows up to 25 m tall.  Smaller with a rounded crown in open habitats. The trunk is smooth and pale grey, often with horizontal ridges.
Inconspicuous small flowers appear before the new leaves in spring. 
The new leaves are light green and hairy, but they become darker and smoother later. The leaves are alternate, have three distinct main veins from the base, and they are rounded and untoothed near the base but toothed for the upper two-thirds.  Some yellowing of the leaves in mid-summer is common.
The fruit is  small and round, green at first but turning yellow to yellowish-brown.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in all 9 provinces of South Africa.
Also native to Africa as far north as Ethiopia.

fields.Family: CANNABACEAE, the Cannabis or Hemp family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Celtis: the name used by Pliny, the Roman author and naturalist
sinensis: from China
fields.Description:
It is often confused with the White Stinkwood, Celtis africana, with which it hybridises.  If the tree is not the White Stinkwood, it should be seen as Celtis sinensis or a hybrid between the two species.
C. africana has softer leaves, they are NOT glossy and they are slightly hairy. 
The leaves of C. sinensis are characteristically dark-green and glossy and it has a darker grey bark.
The fruit of C. sinensis is similar to that of C. africana but they turn dark orange and mature to red-brown during autumn.
fields.Notes:
Not a listed Invasive, but it should be!  It is often confused with Celtis africana, with which it hybridises. It is common in our reserves.
CONTROL:  Cut the plants down to just above the ground and paint the stump immediately with Kaput.  Don't use excessive amounts of Kaput and be careful not to spill it or get it straight onto the soil.
Indigenous to China, Korea, Japan and Taiwan.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cereus: from the Greek ‘κηρός’ meaning wax, torch or candle.
jamacaru: is a corruption of the common name used in Brazil, 'Mandacaru'.
fields.Description:
Cactus plants are easily identified by the presence of small, often hairy cushion-like structures and, in almost all species, with spines growing from them.
It is a leafless, succulent tree up to ±5 metres high.  C. jamacaru, itself is very thorny but there are several hybrids, some of which are relatively free of thorns.
The flower buds appear in spring and the ±150-250 mm, creamy white flowers open at dusk.  Each flower lasts for one night and it withers by quite early morning. 
The purplish-red fruit is egg-shaped and ±90-120 x 60-80 mm. It splits down on one side showing the white pulp and tiny black seeds.
fields.Notes:
A SERIOUS Category 1b INVASIVE.  
It is indigenous to Brazil and common in the north-east of that country. 
Biological control is possible using the Cactus mealybug, Hypogeococcus pungens (see photo)

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Chaetacanthus: possibly 'Chaetos' (hair) and 'ákanthos' (thorn).
costatus: meaning rib.
fields.Description:
A many branched perennial.  its branches are covered with very fine hairs.
Its leaves are ±10 x 4-5 mm but sometimes narrower.
The flowers are borne in the axils of the leaves.  The calyx has 5 narrow sharp-ponted lobes. The corolla is tubular with two upper lips and three longer lower lips, white often with some pale purple shading or markings.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Endemic to South Africa (i.e. it doesn't occur naturally elsewhere) 
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Chamaecrista: from two Greek words, 'chamae', (low growth) and 'crista' 'crested.'
mimosoides: lika a Mimosa.
fields.Description:
A small herb up to 200 mm high, taller in favourable conditions.
It has finely divided pinnate leaves, with leaflets arranged on each side of a common axis.
The flowers are small, about 3 mm across borne on the internode above the axil of the leaf.
The fruit is a green pod with reddish edges darkening with age.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape, Free State and Northern Cape.
Widespread in warm temperate and tropical Africa and Asia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cheilanthes: from the Greek words, 'cheilos' - lip and 'anthos' - flower (interesting for a plant that doesn't have flowers). 
viridis: meaning green
fields.Description:
Ferns produce spores not seeds and the spores are carried in a structure called a sorus (plural sori).  
The fronds of Cheilanthes are carried on hairless, dark brown to black stems that can be up to 200 mm long.
The frond is branched and the green leaflets are carried on the lateral branches of the frond. There may be separate leaflets on the lateral stem or joined together.  
The sori of Cheilanthes are light brown and they are arranged along the edges of the leaflets.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape and Western Cape.
Also in east Africa and parts of Asia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Chenopodium: from the Ancient Greek χήν 'khḗn' (goose), and πούς 'poús' (foot).
album: from the Latin (white).
fields.Description:
A fast-growing annual weed.
Initially it is upright, but due to the weight of the leaves, flowers and fruit, it needs the support of by other plants to remain upright. 
The leaves are alternate and varied in appearance. The first leaves are usually toothed and roughly diamond-shaped, 30-60 mm long and 25-50 mm broad. The leaves on the upper part of the flowering stems are usually smaller and less wide. The flowers are small and grow on on a dense inflorescence 70–200 mm long.
fields.Notes: This plant is native to parts of Europe although its range is not certain.  In the reserves of Pretoria it is a WEED that has almost certainly been dumped by someone together with their garden refuse.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Chironia: named after Chiron, the good, ‘civilised’ centaur of Greek mythology who studied medicine, astronomy, music and other arts.
palustris: of marshy places
fields.Description:
This erect perennial herb grows up to 600 mm high.  The stems are often 4-ridged. 
It forms a basal rosette of broad, spoon-shaped leaves, while the leaves higher up the stems are long and narrow ±20-60mm long and 5-10 mm wide.  They are bluish-green.  
The flowers are mauve to bright pink or red about 30 mm across in 5-18 flowered inflorescences.  The anthers are bright yellow and 4-7 mm long.
The fruit is ±7-12 mm long and quite narrow.
fields.Notes: NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria, always in damp areas.

fields.Common Names: Does not have a widely-used specific common name
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Chlorophytum: from the Greek 'chloros' (green) and 'phyton' (plant).
transvaalense: from the Transvaal.
fields.Description:
An erect perennial herb.
its leaves are long and ±5 mm wide with no clear midrib.
The flower stem is upright and up to ±300 mm tall. 
The flower buds are white and striped with light brown. The starry flowers have six petals and have prominent stamens and ovary.
The fruit is a pointed capsule.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Free State.
Also indigenous to Eastern Zimbabwe, Swaziland and southern Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cirsium: from the Greek word kirsos, which is said to mean swollen vein, referring to thistles being used as a remedy against swollen veins.
vulgare: from the Latin meaning 'common'.
fields.Description:
A tall biennial (i.e. it completes its life cycle in two years), although it sometimes flowers and sets seeds in the first year.  It forms a basal rosette of leaves the first year and flowers and seeds the second year.
The flowering stems can reach 1-1.5 metres. They are winged, with many spiny wings along their full length. 
The leaves are spear-shaped, dark green, with stiff hairs above and white woolly below. They are deeply lobed, with the lobes ending in strong spines.
The base of the flower head is egg-shaped, with many spiny, green bracts that curl outwards.  The florets are purplish pink and tubular.
The seed head consists of many seeds, each with a stiff hair-like structure at the top (a bit like a parachute), called a pappus.  The pappus hairs are feathery.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE.
It is originally from Europe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Clematis: from the Greek, meaning vine branch.
brachiata: at right angles, arm-like.
fields.Description:
This vigorous climbing plant is deciduous (i.e. it loses its leaves in winter).  The bark on the thin stems often peels away.
The leaves are opposite and divided into compound leaflets.  The leaves and petioles (leaf stems) curl around other plants to support the new growth.  
The creamy white flowers appear at the end of summer and they have bright yellow stamens.
They are followed by seed heads that look like a spider, with each seed having a long feathery curling tailthat helps the seeds to disperse.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs mainly in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal it also found in Eastern Cape, Northern Cape and Western Cape. Widespread in Africa and parts of Asia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cleome:
from the Greek 'kleos' meaning glory.
 monophylla: from the Greek ‘mono’ (one) and 'phylla' (leaf) - many Cleomes have compound leaves.
fields.Description:
A small, upright annual herb ±150 mm high, that flowers in late summer. 
The stems, leaves and fruit are slightly hairy. 
The leaves are simple (i.e. not divided into leaflets), long and narrow.
The inflorescences (flower heads) are terminal. 
The flowers are mauve with purple and yellow markings on the petals. 
The fruit is a long thin capsule (a dry fruit that splits open to release the seed) and is usually slightly curved.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.  Widespread in much of Africa and in parts of Asia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Coccinia: Coccinia from Latin coccineus meaning red.
sessilifolia: meaning without a leaf stem.
fields.Description:
A perennial herbaceous climber, with a woody underground tuber. It produces hairless, bluish-green, shoots up to 4 metres long with tendrils.  
Its hairless leaves have five distinct lobes and are darker green above and paler green underneath.  Despite its specific name it usually has a leaf stem. 
The flowers are a wide trumpet-shape, creamy to dark yellow, with green veins and hairy. 
The fruit is ±80-120 mm × 25-40 mm, initially green with white longitudinal spots or stripes turning orange and then red.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, Free State and the western part of Northern Cape.
Also indigenous to Namibia and Botswana

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Combretum: the name given by Pliny to a climbing plant.
erythrophyllum: meaning red leaf, referring to the reddish leaf colour in autumn.
fields.Description:
A medium-sized tree that can reach 10-12 metres in good conditions.  The wood is soft and was used by the Voortrekkers for brake blocks on their oxwagons.
Young trees have a light brown bark but this changes as the bark flakes off in places giving it a mottled appearance.  Old trees often develop growths on the stem and main branches.
The leaves are ±60-90 x 20-40 mm, light green turning yellowish to reddish brown in autumn.
The flower spikes are ±20 x 12 mm and creamy white. 
The fruit is ±12-20 mm across.  It is a four-winged samara typical of the Combretums, starting green but turning light brown in the autumn and often persisting on the tree until spring.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the Pretoria area and common along the rivers of Pretoria. 
NATIVE to Faerie Glen, Moreleta Spruit 
INTRODUCED to Kruin Park

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Combretum: the name given by Pliny to a climbing plant.
molle: from the Latin `mollis' (soft and hairy.)
fields.Description:
A tree of medium height with brown to greyish brown bark.
The leaves are simple (not divided into leaflets) and ovate (egg-shaped). The immature leaves have fine, soft hairs giving them a velvety feel.
The inflorescences (flower heads) are made up of many mustard yellow flowers which appear in spring.
The four-winged fruits develop in summer and turn reddish in autumn.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.  Widespread in tropical and warm temperate Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Combretum: the name given by Pliny to a climbing plant.
zeyheri: in honour of K.L.P. Zeyher, a German botanist who was active in South Africa in the early 19th century.
fields.Description:
A fine tree of medium height with greyish-brown bark.
The leaves are simple (not divided into leaflets) more or less hairless, wavy edged and with quite prominent veins.
The inflorescence (flower head) consists of many greenish yellow flowers and these appear in spring.
The four-winged fruit is large (about 60 mm) green at first but turning brown later.
The leaves turn dark golden brown in autumn.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to many reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal. Also native to Africa as far north as the DRC and Kenya.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Commelina: named after the Dutch botanist Jan Commelijn
africana: from Africa
fields.Description:
A spreading, perennial herb up to 500 mm high but much less in drier places.
The leaves are variable, sessile (i.e. with no leaf stem), oblong to linear, flat or folded, 60-90 mm long, sometimes hairless and sometimes pubescent (downy, with short, soft, erect hairs).
The inflorescence (flower head) is enclosed in a single, folded, green, leaflike spathe that is often sickle-shaped. 
Four varieties have been described, all very similar and difficult to tell apart (I believe the plants in Kruin Park are mostly Commelina africana var. barberae, but for our purposes a yellow Commelina is Commelina africana). 
It flowers in late summer and the flowers have usually faded by noon.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape and Western Cape.  Also occurs across Africa and into the Arabian Peninsula.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Commelina: after the Dutch botanist Jan Commelijn
benghalensis: from Benghal
fields.Description:
A spreading perennial. 
Its leaves are ±60 mm long and ±35mm wide, and shiny.  The base of the leaf has long bristles that are usually dark reddish-brown and it wraps around the stem.
The inflorescence (flower head) is enclosed in a velvety or slightly hairy green leaf-like spathe.
The flowers are small, ±10 mm across and blue; they open in the morning and don't last all day.
fields.Notes:
A WEED, probably introduced to reserves in Pretoria.
Originally discovered and collected in India, it is indigenous to tropical Africa and Asia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Commelina: after the Dutch botanist Jan Commelijn
eckloniana: after Christian Ecklon, a Danish pharmacist and botanist
fields.Description:
A spreading perennial. Stems often root at the nodes. 
Leaves are variable, narrowly lanceolate, 50-100 mm long, sessile (i.e. with no leaf stem), velvety or slightly hairy. 
The inflorescence (flower head) is enclosed in a velvety or slightly hairy green leaf-like spathe.
It's flowers are blue here in Kruin Park, open in the morning and don't last all day.
The blue Commelinas are difficult to tell apart.  The photos are of a plant that is definitely C. eckloniana
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, and Eastern Cape.  It is also found beyond our boundaries.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Convolvulus: from the Latin "convolvere", (to twine around).
sagittatus: from the Latin (arrow-shaped.)
fields.Description:
A variable perennial, prostrate in open grassland but twining up fences and other plants.
Its leaves are often sagittate (shaped like the head of an arrow).
The white to pink flowers are about 10-25 mm and they appear in spring.
The fruit is light brown and rounded capsule (i.e. it splits open to release the seed)
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Widespread in every province of South Africa.
Also occurs in Africa as far north as Sudan.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Conyza: a name used by Pliny and Dioscorides for a type of Fleabane. 
podocephala: from the Greek 'podos' (food) and 'cephala' (head.)
fields.Description:
A spreading perennial generally 200-400mm high.
The leaves have rough hairs and are scalloped toward the top of the leaf.
The flower heads are solitary on long stems.
The seed head consists of many seeds, each with a  stiff hair-like structure, called a pappus, attached to the top.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Northern Cape and Eastern Cape.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cotoneaster: Apparently from cotoneus an old Latin name for the quince.
franchetii: named after Adrien René Franchet, a French botanist at the Paris Muséum National d’Histoire Naturelle.
fields.Description:
An evergreen shrub growing to ±2 metres tall. 
The leaves are oval, ±20-30 mm long and 10-15 mm wide.  They are green above but downy below with dense whitish hairs. 
The flowers are produced in clusters of 5 or more; each flower is 6-7 mm across, with five pink to white petals,
The  fruits are like small, reddish-orange apples, 6-8 mm in diameter.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE.
Indigenous to south-western China, Myanmar and Thailand.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cotyledon: from the Greek 'kotyledon' (a cup-shaped hollow) referring to the leaves of some species.
orbiculata: from the Latin circular.
fields.Description:
An evergreen, succulent shrublet usually ±600-800 mm tall.
The leaves are smooth, round and grey-green, often edged with red.
The pinkish-orange to red flowers are pendulous and are on long stalks. They appear from June to August.
fields.Notes:
NOT native to the Pretoria area.  INTRODUCED to some reserves in Pretoria. 
Indigenous to Namaqualand, Karoo regions and rocky outcrops in areas with low rainfall.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Crabbea: named for the British amateur botanist and poet Rev. George Crabbe.
angustifolia: from the Latin words, 'angustus' (narrow) and 'folia' (leaves.)
fields.Description:
A prostrate herb with long narrow leaves that often have wavy edges and some hairs along the margins.
The white to cream flowers are borne in a head among large spiny bracts.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in grassland in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, and KwaZulu-Natal.  Also found in south-eastern Botswana

fields.Common Names: Tree Crassula, Silver Dollar Plant, Beestebal
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Crassula: from the Latin crassus, meaning fat.
arborescens: tree-like.
fields.Description:
A small to medium-sized succulent shrub often with a single stem and with many branches.
The leaves are thick and fleshy, distinctly grey-green and often with reddish margins.
The flowers are white to pink and star-shaped and they turn brown after they are pollinated.
The fruit is a follicle (like a pod but splitting one only one side) ±6mm long.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to several reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape and the drier parts of Western Cape. Also native to Swaziland.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Crassula: from the Latin crassus, meaning fat.
capitella, is derived from the Latin capitellum, which means 'small head
fields.Description:
An extremely variable species. 
a small, succulent herb, it is a variable species ±100-400 mm high, sometimes upright and at other times sprawling and forming a mat. Stems that lie on the ground often take root. Each stem forms roots at its internodes, which take root if the stem lies against the ground.
The leaves are in opposite pairs, fleshy, quite narrow and pointed, green but becoming red in full sunlight.
Near the top of a rosette, the leaves gradually get smaller and change into floral bracts, as the stem forms a long, pointed inflorescence (flower stem).
It flowers in the summer, with small, white flowers at intervals up the flower stem.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to several reserves in Pretoria.
The few plants that I found in a Pretoria reserve appeared to have come from garden rubbish dumped close to one of the gates.
According to the SANBI website, it is native to all of South Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Crassula: from the Latin crassus, meaning fat.
multicava: from the Latin multi, meaning many, and cava, hollow, hole or cavity. referring to the many little holes that can be seen on the leaves.
fields.Description:
A prostrate, evergreen succulent that forms mats up to ±300 mm.
The leaves are in opposite pairs, oval to round ±15-25 mm long and 12-20mm wide.  They are light to dark green in their native habitat but often purplish when growing in dry conditions. The leaves have numerous modified pores, especially on a leaf, which exudes drops of water.
The flower buds are pink and the flowers, which appear in masses above the leaves, are white to pink and are shaped like a 5 pointed star.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to several reserves in Pretoria.
NOT native to the Pretoria area.  
Indigenous to Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape and eastern parts of Western Cape, where it grows on forest edges and river banks.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Crassula: from the Latin crassus, meaning fat.
ovata: a reference to the egg-shaped leaves.
fields.Description:
A branched shrub growing up to 3 metres, but about 700 mm high in Kruin Park
The stems are succulent and brownish-grey
The leaves have no leaf stems, are ±25-50 x 18-30 mm, glossy green in the rainy season but shrivelled and purplish in the dry season.
The flowers are in flattish terminal inflorescences (the arrangement of the flowers). They have white or faint pink, 5-petalled, star-shaped flowers.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to several reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.
Also occurs in Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Crotalaria: from the Ancient Greek κρόταλον, meaning "castanet".
agatiflora: with flowers like those of Agati, an old generic name for Sesbania.
fields.Description:
An evergreen shrub up to ±2-3 m tall in Kruin Park.  The young shoots are slightly hairy. 
The leaves are greyish-green, with three leaflets on a short stalk
The flowers are carried on 300-400 mm, many-flowered racemes right through the summer.  They are lemon-yellow to greenish-yellow, with a projecting greenish or purple beak.
The fruit is an inflated greenish-purple pod inflated, ±80-100 mm long and the seeds rattle in the pod once it is dry.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE.
CONTROL: It can be controlled by cutting it down about 10-20 mm above the ground and painting the cut stump with Kaput.
ORIGIN: It is native to Tropical East Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cryptolepis: meaning of the name - uncertain
oblongifolia: from the Latin (oblong-leafed).
fields.Description:
A small shrub with many stems, often sprawling on other plants, 500 mm-1 m high usually with long, slender, reddish-brown branches. 
The leaves are in pairs, elliptic-oblong, 250-500 mm long, 150-250 mm wide, hairless, darkish green above and paler beneath.  The petiole (leaf stem) varies from 5-20 mm long. 
The flowers are in clusters, greenish-yellow and about 3mm across. 
The fruit is a pair of long follicles (pod-like but splitting along only one seam) joined at the base so that they look like horns.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.  It also occurs in much of Africa southwards from Sierra Leone and Sudan.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cuscuta: of Arabic derivation meaning "dodder".
campestris: of the fields.
fields.Description:
A parasitic plant, after the seed germinates it develops a rudimentary root for anchorage. Very soon the plant produce tendrils that attach to the host plant.  The root and shoot below this initial attachment soon die, leaving no direct contact with the soil. 
The plant then develops a network of leafless, smooth, yellow or orange stems ±3 mm in diameter.
The flowers are in groups of 3-8.  They are bell-shaped with 4 or 5 petals joined at the base and 2-2.5 mm across.
The fruit is a depressed spherical capsule, light brown or brownish, ±1-1.5 mm.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE.
It can be difficult to control because it twines around the host plant.
It should be sprayed when still young and it covers a small area, so that damage to surrounding plants can be limited.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cussonia: named after Pierre Cusson, professor of botany at the University of Montpellier in France.
paniculata: referring to the way that the flowers are carried on branches of the main axis.
fields.Description:
A short thickset tree up to about 5 metres.  It has deeply fissured dark brown bark.
The palmately compound leaves are clustered at the ends of the branches and have a long petiole (leaf stem). 
The small, green flowers appear in late summer and are carried on short stalks in dense spikes that make up a large, branched inflorescence at the end of the trunk or branches. 
The flowers are followed by fleshy, purple-maroon fruits, which ripen in autumn and early winter.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Groenkloof Nature Reserve and other reserves. 
It occurs inland at high altitudes from the mountains of the Karoo and Eastern Cape through KwaZulu-Natal and Free State into Gauteng and further north.   Also native to Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cussonia: the name given by Carl Peter Thunberg to commemorate the French botanist Pierre Cusson. 
spicata:  referring to the unbranched inflorescence in which the flowers are without stalks.
fields.Description:
Initially a slender tree becoming thickset later with a much branched, rounded crown.  
Leaf scars remain visible on the stems of young plants after which the trunk becomes grey to light brown.  Finally, with age, the bark becomes rough. 
The leaves are large and on long leaf stems, they are glossy dark green, alternate, and palmate (with the leaflets spreading from a common centre, like the fingers of a hand).  
The inflorescence is a sturdy candle-like spike.  The small greenish flowers are insignificant and have 5 petals. 
The fruits turn black when ripe and they attract birds.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to several reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to southern and eastern South Africa.
Also occurs in eastern Zimbabwe, Mozambique and northwards to tropical Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Cymbopogon:  from the Greek 'kymbe' (a boat) and 'pogon' (a beard). In most species, the hairy spikelets project from boat-shaped spathes.
fields.Description:
A perennial tuft grass up to 1,800 mm high.
The leaves are bluish grey.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to several reserves in Pretoria. Not a listed invasive but UNDOUBTEDLY BECOMING INVASIVE.
Native to Tropical Asia

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cynanchum: from the Greek 'kynos' (dog) and 'anchein', (to choke).
viminale: from the Latin 'vimen' (a pliant twig) referring to the weeping habit of the branches.
fields.Description:
A very variable succulent vine.  Its stems and branches scramble over or climb into other vegetation.  They are grey-green and produce milky sap when broken. 
The leaves are reduced to scales. 
The flowers are in roughly spherical clusters and they appear in mid-summer. 
The fruits are carrot-shaped and they contain seeds each with a tuft of white, silky hairs.
A more prostrate form of the Milk Rope occurs in some reserves.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to several reserves in Pretoria.
According to SANBI's Threatened Species Programme http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=2649-2 it is native to Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape and Western Cape (thus excluding Gauteng)
Cynanchum viminale occurs in Africa and southern Asia,

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cynodon: from the Greek, ‘cyon’ (dog) and “dónti’ (tooth)
dactylon: with fingers
fields.Description:
A perennial grass that spreads by means of underground stems (stolons) forming roots at each node.
The lower part of the leaf forms a sheath with a ring of short hairs at the base of the leaf blade.  The leaf blade is bluish-green and flat with a sharp tip. 
The flower stems consist of 3-7 slender spikes and they appear in late summer.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Kruin Park, Colbyn Valley.
Widespread in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, Free State, Eastern Cape and Western Cape.

fields.Family: BORAGINACEAE, the Borage and Forget-me-not family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cynoglossum: from the Greek word 'cynos', (of a dog) and 'glossa', (tongue).
lanceolatum: lance or spear-shaped.
fields.Description:
An upright, biennial plant usually growing up to ±900 mm tall, but smaller in Kruin Park.
The lower leaves are ±100 mm long and ±10x12 mm wide, smaller higher up and on short leaf stems.
The tiny flowers are blue to violet and carried on a long, arching spike.
The fruit is a small nut, densely covered with bulbous-based hooked hairs.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Gauteng, possibly introduced to Kruin Park.  A troublesome plant because its seeds cling to clothing and to animals.
Indigenous to Africa south of the Sahara, the Arabian Peninsula and much of southern Asia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Cyperus:  κύπειρος kypeiros, the Greek name, for several species. 
sexangularis: from the Latin, six-angled.
fields.Description:
A evergreen perennial herb of wetland areas, it produces upright stems that are more or less triangular in cross-section with a line or rib down the centre of each face.
The leaves are linear ±120-180 x 12-20 mm and they are in a whorl at the top of the stems.  
The flowers are yellowish to reddish-brown and appear among the leaves in early summer.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Colbyn Valley wetland reserve and probably other wetland areas.
It occurs in moist conditions in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape and Northern Cape.
Also in tropical Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Dichapetalum: Probably a reference to the plant’s forked petals
cymosum: a reference to the cymose grouping of the flowers, where the flowers are attached to a main stem, each side branch ends in a flower and the terminal flower opens first.
fields.Description:
A small sub-shrub with erect unbranched stems.  It has a large, woody, underground rhizome. 
The fresh young leaves that appear early in the spring contain a poison that is lethal to cattle.
The leaves have very short stalks and they are green but paler green beneath, almost hairless and ±50–120 x 20-30 mm.  The veins are prominent and they “turn back” from the leaf margins.
The sepals (i.e. the outer whorls of the flower) are narrow, ±7 mm long, free almost to the base. The creamy-whitish petals are narrowly oblong, ±7 mm long, and forked for 2/3 of their length.
The plant rarely produces fruits.  They are more or less egg-shaped and brownish-yellow.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.
Also indigenous to the Caprivi in Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, and Zambia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Dichilus: from the Greek δις (twice) and χείλη (lipped)
lebeckioides: Lebeckia-like
fields.Description:
An untidy deciduous shrub ±500 mm tall. 
The leaves are compound with three leaflets  ±10-15 x2-3 mm.
The flowers are typical of the bean family yellow with some brownish markings.
The fruit is a pod with constrictions between each seed.
fields.Notes:
There are a few plants of this taxon growing in the introduced soil on the terrace south of the Muckleneuk reservoir in the Kruin Park Nature Reserve 
It is indigenous to Free State, Gauteng, Limpopo, Mpumalanga, Northern Cape, North West and also Botswana

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Dichrostachys: from the Greek, 'dis' (two); 'chroos', (colour); and 'stachys', (spike).
cinerea: from the Latin (ash-coloured).
fields.Description:
A deciduous tree, ±2 metres high and generally with quite thin stems. 
Young stems soon develop smooth greyish brown bark.  Later secondary thickening of the branches and main stems leads to deep fissures in the rough, light greyish bark.
The bipinnately compound (twice compound) leaves are carried on long petioles (leaf stems).  They have between 4 and 15 pinnae (leaf segments) and each pinna has between 9 and 35 leaflets.
The “flower” is actually an inflorescence made up of many sterile pink flowers and fertile yellow flowers. They hang from the axils of the leaves in early summer.  
Clusters of twisted pods turn mustard brown in autumn.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to many reserves in Pretoria.
Dichrostachys cinerea is a complex species with several sub-species in South Africa. It is widespread in Africa.

fields.Common Names: Large Wild Iris, Fairy Iris, Groot Wilde Iris
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Dietes: meaning having two relatives, a reference to the relationship between Dietes and Moraea and Iris.
grandiflora: means large flower
fields.Description:
An evergreen perennial with long, rigid, dark green leaves ±800-1000 mm high
