The flowers are carried on slender stems about as tall as the leaves.  They have three, white, more or less upright “standards” and three horizontal “falls” that are white each with a golden yellow bar.  A further three “petals” are light mauve.
The fruit is a capsule that splits along three lines to release the ripe seeds.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to some nature reserves in Pretoria.
NOT indigenous to Gauteng, indigenous to KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Diospyros: from the Greek 'dios' (of Zeus) and 'pyros' (grain). 
lycioides: resembles a plant called Lycium.
fields.Description:
Diospyros is a deciduous shrub and in favourable situations a small tree up to 5 metres tall.
Its egg-shaped leaves have a sharp point and are velvety with prominent veins.
The small (± 3 mm) bell-shaped flowers are pale yellow and are followed by green spherical fruits (± 15 mm) that turn red.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several nature reserves in Pretoria.
D. lycioides is widespread in all of South Africa except the winter rainfall part of the Western Cape.
D. lycioides subsp. guerkii occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Dodonaea: named in honour of Rembert Dodoens, a 16th century Flemish botanist, royal physician, and professor. 
viscosa: from the Latin, meaning sticky, referring to the texture of the leaves.
fields.Description:
An evergreen shrub, or a small tree up to ±2-3 metres in Kruin Park, usually multi-stemmed.
The bark is dark grey and stringy.  
The leaves are alternate, narrowly elliptic (±70-100 x 25-30 mm) and shiny light green.
The flowers are greenish-yellow in dense inflorescences.
The fruit develops 2-3 papery wings.  They start green but turn pale yellow and then red.
fields.Notes:
Dodonaea viscosa is a variable species that is NATIVE to EVERY CONTINENT except Antarctica. Research tells us that it evolved in Australia from its most recent common ancestor in the Late Pliocene to Early Pleistocene.
 The seeds of Sand Olive germinate easily and it readily becomes dominant where it occurs in a Pretoria reserve.
It is grown worldwide to stabilise sand dunes and to control erosion, which probably explains how it has spread throughout South Africa.  It has been coastal KwaZulu-Natal, and to the coast and mountains of Eastern Cape and Western Cape (even quite arid regions). (See for example Coates Palgrave, K., Trees of Southern Africa)

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Dolichandra: meaning uncertain.
unguis-cati: unguis (nail or claw) and cati (of a cat).
fields.Description:
A rampant climber with claw-like tendrils that cling to trees and other plants for support.
The leaves are opposite and in pairs.
The attractive, yellow trumpet-shaped flowers appear in spring.
These are followed by long flat pods that rupture and shed a host of flat seeds that are carried by wind.
fields.Notes:
A SERIOUS Category 1b INVASIVE, likely to remain a problem in Pretoria's reserves because there are many in nearby gardens and the seeds are blown into the reserve.
CONTROL:  Control of Cat’s Claw Creeper is problematical, not because herbicides don’t work but because the relevant government department has not registered anything for its control (which means that it’s against the law to use the products that do work).
Cut the plants down close to the ground and wait for some regrowth.  Then TARGET SPRAY to avoid spraying other plants, using one of about 10 herbicides containing Triclopyr.
Glyphosate (widely sold as RoundUp) is still readily available but this might change.  Until then, in the home garden, cut the plants down close to the ground, wait for some regrowth and then TARGET SPRAY or paint the new leaves with Glyphosate.
As is the case with Pompom Weed, a product containing Picloram is NOT appropriate in a nature area.
Native to the forests of Central America, South America and the Caribbean.

fields.Family: BORAGINACEAE, the Borage and Forget-me-not family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ehretia: the name honours the German botanical illustrator Georg Dionysius Ehret.
rigida: from the Latin (stiff, rigid, hard or inflexible).
fields.Description:
Usually a shrub or small tree up to 2 metres high, it can grow bigger.
The bark is smooth and grey on new branches and rough on older branches and stems. 
The leaves are alternate (not in pairs) often at the tips of its short branches. They are sometimes smooth and at other times, they have rough hairs.
The 6-9 mm flowers appear in spring in dense clusters on the branches. 
The 4-5 mm fruits are round, green at first, then orange to red, and they turn black when ripe.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Pretoria's nature reserves.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape and Western Cape.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Elephantorrhiza: meaning elephant root.
elephantina: also a reference to the size of the huge underground part of this plant.
fields.Description:
The Elephant's Root is not what one expects.  It appears to be no more than one or more leaves each with a stem, 6 or more lateral stems, more stems on them and many small leaflets.  
In fact, it’s much more.  Everything above the ground is the canopy of a large and sometimes huge underground tree.
The “flower” is actually an inflorescence made up of many pale yellowish white flowers that turn golden yellow.  The inflorescences are arranged in the axils of the leaves and are usually carried close to the ground or protruding from ground level.  
The fruits are large dark brown or reddish-brown pods suspended just above the ground.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Pretoria's nature reserves.
Occurs in much of South Africa except the winter rainfall part of Western Cape.  It also occurs further north.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Eleusine: ---
indica: from India
fields.Description:
A prostrate and spreading annual grass, very rarely rooting at the nodes. The root system is very well developed and strong hence the common name Jongosgras. 
It is often found in lawns because it is easily confused with Kikuyu Grass.
fields.Notes:
An uncommon WEED in some reserves.
Native to temperate and tropical Asia and parts of Africa.  
Now it is distributed almost throughout the tropical world 
It invades disturbed habitats in natural areas and it is also a common weed along roads and sidewalks.

fields.Scientific Name: Englerophytum magalismontanum, previously Bequaertiodendron magalismontanum and before that Chrysophyllum magalismontanum
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Englerophytum: meaning  Engler's tree, after Prof. H.G.A. Engler, a German botanist and renowned authority on African plants.
magalismontanum: of the Magaliesberg.
fields.Description:
This is a small to medium size evergreen shrub or tree, usually from 3-5 metres.
It often branches close to the ground level and the leaves are often crowded at the end of branches. 
New growth, both leaves and shoots, have a rusty appearance caused by russet-brown hairs.  
Older leaves are rolled under at the margins, glossy dark green above but covered with a whitish bloom that can be rubbed off.  The reverse of the leaf is densely covered with silky golden brown hairs.  The midrib is prominent. 
The small flowers are carried on mature stems and branches.  The sepals (outer whorl of the flower) are brownish and the petals are greenish-yellow.
The edible fruit is a roundish or elliptical berry (like a tomato), turning yellowish and then red.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several of Pretoria's nature reserves.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.  Also native to Botswana, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Malawi and Swaziland.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Erigeron: one source suggests that this is from the Greek eri, early or perhaps erio, woolly and geron, old man. (I cannot confirm this)
canadensis: of Canada
fields.Description:
An annual plant, usually 600-900 mm tall in Kruin Park.
The stems are sparsely hairy. 
The leaves have no leaf stem, are ±200mm long x ±10-20mm wide, with toothed margins.  The lower leaves tend to wither early.
Typical of the Daisy family, the flower is actually a bunch of tiny flowers.  Each “flower” of Canadian fleabane has a ring of tiny whitish ray florets and a centre of yellow disk florets. 
The fruit is a also typical, a dandelion-like head ±15mm across of little parachute-like seeds.
fields.Notes:
A WEED that is common on derelict land, the seeds blow in the wind.
Native to much of North and Central America.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Erythrina: from the Greek word ερυθρός (erythros) meaning red.
lysistemon: means “with loose stamen or stamens”.
fields.Description:
A sturdy deciduous tree up to ±10 or more metres tall.
The bark is smooth and dark grey to grey-brown, with some short, hooked thorns on the trunk and branches. 
The compound leaves have three ±120-150mm leaflets).  The leaf stems and the midribs also have hooked thorns. 
The flowers develop in early spring before the new leaves or as the leaves begin to show.
The fruit is a pod with a distinct constriction between each seed and the seeds are bright red.
fields.Notes:
Native to the Pretoria area but it has been INTRODUCED to some of Pretoria's reserves. 
E. lysistemon is native to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga KwaZulu-Natal and the eastern part of Eastern Cape.  
Also native to Botswana, Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Swaziland

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Euclea: from the Greek word 'eukleia' (glory and fame), referring to the fine ebony-like wood of some species.
crispa: refers to the wavy edges of the leaves.
fields.Description:
Evergreen tree up to 5 metres.
The branches are grey while the young stems are brown.
The leaves vary from long and narrow to elliptical where the leaf is about 3 times as long as it is wide.  They sometimes have a wavy edge, but they always have translucent veins.
The small creamy white flowers appear in early summer.
The fruit is a small reddish berry (like a tomato)
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several of Pretoria's reserves.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape and parts of Western Cape.  It is also native to Angola, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Malawi, Lesotho and Swaziland.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Eulophia: from the Greek 'eu' (good) and 'lophos' (crest) referring to the crest on the lip.
ovalis: from the Medieval Latin, ovalis (oval-shaped)
fields.Description:
The inflorescence is a spike. 
The flowers have two whorls of petal-like elements. 
The outer whorl has three purplish sepals and the inner whorl, which is predominantly white to pale mauve, has two lateral petals and a lip. 
The lateral petals are white to pale mauve and the lip is white with blue markings towards the centre. The central part of the lip has a creamy yellow patch with slender, protuberances.
The lip is irregularly shaped, the lower part is wider and there are two smaller lip lobes deeper in the flower.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in the Pretoria area.
Occurs predominantly in eastern North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, northern Free State and eastern Cape. Also in southern Limpopo and eastern Northern Cape.
Also indigenous to Lesotho and Swaziland.

fields.Family: EUPHORBIACEAE, the Euphorbia or Poinsettia family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Euphorbia: in honour of Euphorbus, the Greek physician to King Juba II of Numidia in North Africa, who used the milky sap for medicinal purposes.
cooperi: named after Thomas Cooper, an English plant collec- tor and grower who introduced this species to English Horticulture.
fields.Description:
A succulent tree with branches that grow outwards from the main stem and then turn upwards.
The branches are deeply constricted at intervals. Short thorns are carried on the ridges of the stems.
The unisexual individual flowers are set in an inflorescence called a cyathium, and are surrounded by colourful, petal-like  bracts.  These are massed along the ridges at the top of the branches.
The fruit is a three-celled capsule that splits open along three lines to release the seed.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several of Pretoria's reserves.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.  Also found beyond our borders.

fields.Family: EUPHORBIACEAE, the Euphorbia or Poinsettia family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Euphorbia: in honour of Euphorbus, the Greek physician to King Juba II of Numidia in North Africa, who used the milky sap for medicinal purposes. 
grantii: in honour of explorer James Augustus Grant
fields.Description:
An upright, evergreen shrub or small tree, up to 3 or 4 metres tall in Kruin Park.
The main stem is ±50-75 mm thick but can be up to ±150 mm thick with a pale greyish bark.  Young stems and branches are hairless, green to purplish and they have a milky sap.  Initially they are fleshy, but they become woody with age.
The leaves are mainly at the tips of the branches, slightly alternate, ±150 mm long and 30-60 mm wide, hairless and can be green to deep wine red. They have a very short leaf stem or none at all.
The leaf margins may have tiny teeth towards the apex and are flat or lightly wavy. The leaves shrivel in our dry winters.
The saucer-shaped flowers are 6.5 mm in diameter, and 2 mm deep and they appear in late winter or spring.  Although they are brownish-red they are quite inconspicuous.
The fruits are red, with downy hairs ±7 mm across and on a short stem.
fields.Notes:
A WEED in several reserves with the potential to become a problem plant.
Native to tropical East Africa, mainly Malawi, parts of Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda; it has been introduced to many warm regions where it tends to naturalise.

fields.Family: EUPHORBIACEAE, the Euphorbia or Poinsettia family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Euphorbia: in honour of Euphorbus, the Greek physician to King Juba II of Numidia in North Africa, who used the milky sap for medicinal purposes.
heterophylla: means differing leaves.
fields.Description:
An annual herb ± 400-600 mm tall in Kruin Park with hollow stems and milky sap.
The leaves have variable shapes within and between populations and the leaf stems are often dark red.  The upper leaves may show some red or white but they are usually plain green in the wild.
fields.Notes:
A prolific WEED probably introduced to Kruin Park with dumped garden rubbish.
Native to tropical and sub-tropical America.  It is resistant to many herbicides and it has spread rapidly in many parts of the world.

fields.Family: EUPHORBIACEAE, the Euphorbia or Poinsettia family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Euphorbia: in honour of Euphorbus, the Greek physician to King Juba II of Numidia in North Africa, who used the milky sap for medicinal purposes.
ingens: means huge.
fields.Description:
An upright, succulent tree up to 5 or 6 metres tall in Kruin Park, with a rounded dark green crown,
The branches are segmented with spines running along the ridges of the segments. It produces small, greenish yellow flowers on the ridges of the topmost segment of every branch from autumn to winter. The fruit, a round 3-lobed capsule, turns red to purple when ripening.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, and KwaZulu-Natal.
Also in Eastern Angola, Zimbabwe and Swaziland.

fields.Scientific Name: Euphorbia milii var. splendens, previously Euphorbia splendens
fields.Family: EUPHORBIACEAE, the Euphorbia or Poinsettia family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Euphorbia: in honour of Euphorbus, the Greek physician to King Juba II of Numidia, later King of Mauretania (now part of northwestern Morocco).
milii: in honour of Baron Milius, a former Governor of Réunion
splendens: from the Latin meaning "shining", "gleaming" or brilliant”
fields.Description:
A small very thorny, succulent shrub ±500 mm tall, it has grey-brown stems about 10-12 mm across, armed on all sided with sharp spines of mostly around 10-20 mm long.
A few bright green leaves ±40 x 12 mm are held near the growing tips of the stems.  They drop off after some months, leaving the spiny stems permanently bare until new leaves form on new terminal growth.
Clusters of “flowers” develop in spring and summer on long reddish stalks at the ends of new spiny stems. The individual flowers are tiny, but each flower is surrounded by two ±20 mm red petal-like bracts. 
Fruiting is uncommon, but when fruits occur they will be three-celled capsules that split open along three lines to release the seed.
fields.Notes: NOT indigenous to the Pretoria area. Native to Madagascar.

fields.Family: EUPHORBIACEAE, the Euphorbia or Poinsettia family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Euphorbia: in honour of Euphorbus, the Greek physician to King Juba II of Numidia in North Africa, who used the milky sap for medicinal purposes.
schinzii: named after the Swiss botanist, Hans Schinz.
fields.Description:
A small, spiny succulent, 100-150 mm tall.
The tiny leaves drop off early and the plant seems to be leafless.
The upright, green branches usually have 4 sides, hollowed or grooved down the sides, and brownish ridges that darken over time.  These ridges are constricted at intervals and the paired spines are carried just below the constriction.
The individual flowers of Euphorbias are set within a flowerlike cyathium, and are surrounded by a number of bracts which are yellow and look like petals.
The fruit is a three-celled capsule (i.e. it splits along three lines to release the seed).
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves inn Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West and Gauteng.  Common on the Magaliesberg and in Pretoria.  Found only on the Quartzite ridges.
Also native to Botswana, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Malawi.

fields.Family: EUPHORBIACEAE, the Euphorbia or Poinsettia family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Euphorbia: in honour of Euphorbus, the Greek physician to King Juba II of Numidia, later King of Mauretania (now part of northwestern Morocco).
tirucalli: is the local name from Malabar in India
fields.Description:
A shrub or tree up to 4 metres tall in Kruin Park.  It exudes a milky latex when it is injured. The trunk can grow to ±150 mm thick with wrinkled, grey bark. 
The stems are green, succulent, and are striped with fine longitudinal ridges.
A few ±10 x 1 mm leaves occur on new growth; they have no leaf stem and drop off soon.
The “flower” is ±10 mm across; it is actually a group of several tiny yellow flowers surrounded by cream-coloured bracts.
The fruit is a 3-lobed capsule, ±8 mm across.
fields.Notes:
The origin of this species is not clear. Noad and Birnie suggest that it was introduced to Africa from India pointing out that the name 'tirucalli' is its local name in Malabar (south-western Kerala) in India.  This seems a reasonable supposition.
However, SANBI records its SA distribution as Limpopo, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape, and Palgrave believes it originated in Africa. INTRODUCED to Kruin Park. 
It is not a listed invasive but it has proved to be invasive in Kruin Park nature reserve.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Felicia: a name given by the French botanist Alexandre de Cassini.
muricata: meaning covered with short, growths.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb, up to 200 mm, much branched and woody at the base. 
Leaves needle-like in tufts along the stems. 
The inflorescences, at the tips of the branches are typical of the daisy family a head consisting of a central disk (disk florets) and an outer ray of petal-like ray florets.
The disc florets are yellow, and the ray florets are white. The ray florets are often rolled up in older flower heads.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several of Pretoria's reserves.
Widespread throughout South Africa and further north.

fields.Common Names: Common Wild Fig (Burke's Fig) Gewone Wildevy
fields.Family: MORACEAE, the Mulberry or Fig family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ficus: classical Latin name for the cultivated fig, from the Persian 'fica'. 
burkei: named after Joseph Burke (1812-1873) a British naturalist who collected the type specimen of Ficus burkei from the Magaliesberg in 1841 while on an expedition with Carl Zeyher, a botanical collector.
fields.Description:
The Figs are a variable genus and botanists are not in agreement about their taxonomy.  Some place F. burkei together with F. thonningii, which is a fig of West Africa.  True Ficus thonningii is probably restricted to West Africa.
A medium to large evergreen tree that is quite often a strangler (i.e. the seed germinates at the canopy of the host plant, the tree produces many aerial roots that grow down to the ground) F. burkei can eventually strangle its host tree.  The bark is grey and quite smooth. 
The leaves are alternate and elliptic in shape, ±50-120 mm long, stiff and leathery, shiny green above, dull and paler below; the midrib is prominent and sometimes yellowish and the margins are entire (untoothed). 
The roundish figs are borne singly or in pairs on short stalks in the leaf axils, rarely on bare twigs, ±10-20 mm in diameter, densely hairy to almost hairless, yellowish brown or rarely pink when ripe.
fields.Notes:
One big tree in Kruin Park Nature Reserve - possibly introduced.
The form previously known as Ficus burkei occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.  
Regarded as Ficus thonningii by some.

fields.Family: MORACEAE, the Mulberry or Fig family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ficus: classical Latin name for the cultivated fig, from the Persian 'fica'. 
salicifolia: leaf like a Salix (a willow)
fields.Description:
Pretoria's 1000-year-old Wonderboom is unique, standing about 25 metres high and with a spread of 55 metres. Its branches droop down to the ground, take root and established a new tree.  Around the original tree, which was killed in a fire many years ago, is a circle of first generation daughter trees, another circle of seven second generation daughter trees and there are three third generation daughter trees.
Elsewhere it is a deciduous tree from 2-8 metres with narrower leaves
fields.Notes:
The huge Wonderboom is in the Wonderboom Nature Reserve
The usual form of F. salicifolia occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.
Also indigenous to Botswana and the eastern parts of Africa to Egypt and Yemen and Socotra.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Furcraea: named after Antoine Francois, Comte de Fourcroy, a French chemist.
foetida: means smelling extremely unpleasant.
fields.Description:
An evergreen perennial with leaves arranged in a rosette, it is usually stemless.
The GREEN leaves are up to 3 metres long and thickened. They are sword-shaped, 100-150 mm broad at their widest point, narrowing at the leaf base, and to a sharp spine tip at the apex; the leaf margins are usually thornless.
The flowers are greenish to creamy white, 40 mm long, and strongly scented; they are produced on a large flower stem up to 7.5 metres tall.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1a INVASIVE
Despite its common name, it is not native to Mauritius, it is indigenous to the Caribbean and northern South America.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Galinsoga: named after M. M. Galinsoga, Head of the Madrid Botanical Garden in 1880.
parviflora: from the Latin parvus (small) and flos, flores (flower, flowers)
fields.Description:
An upright, annual herb, ± 200-300 mm tall in the shallow soils of Kruin Park.  
The leaves in opposite pairs.  Only the lower leaves have leaf stems. The leaves are oval with a sharp point. 
The “flower” is typical of the daisy family, Asteraceae, a composite flower head, ±5-8 mm across. It usually consists of five, three-lobed, white ray florets and an inner cluster of yellow, tubular disk florets. 
The seed head consists of several black, one-seeded, fruits each with a pappus (a stiff hair-like structure that acts as a parachute to aid dispersal).
fields.Notes:
An uncommon WEED in our reserves, probably introduced with garden rubbish.
Native to Central America, it is a widespread weed.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Gazania: possibly named after Theodor of Gaza or a reference to the Greek 'gaza' (riches).
krebsiana: after Georg Krebs, a German chemist and botanist.
serrulata: finely toothed.
fields.Description:
A stemless perennial herb growing from a woody rootstock.
Somewhat unusually it has a milky latex.
The linear leaves are green with a white-felted reverse.
The flower heads, which appear in spring are solitary on a bare stalk and the ray florets are while the disk florets are yellow.
The seed head consists of many seeds, each with a  stiff hair-like structure, called a pappus, attached to the top.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Pretoria's reserves.
Gazania krebsiana subsp. serrulata occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, and Mpumalanga.  The yellow form occurs mainly on the Witwatersrand and the white form is found in the Pretoria - Magaliesberg area.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Gerbera: in honour of the German naturalist Traugott Gerber.
viridifolia: meaning green leaves (many Gerberas have leaves covered with pale silky hairs)
fields.Description:
A stemless perennial herb.
The leaves appear from the silky crown and, unlike the rest of the Genus Gerbera, have a green reverse.
The flower heads, which appear in spring and early summer are solitary on a bare stalk.
The ray florets are usually white with a pink reverse and the disk florets are white to pink but white forms occur.
The seed head consists of many seeds, each with a  stiff hair-like structure, called a pappus, attached to the top.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE, ie indigenous, to the nature areas of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape.  Also in Swaziland, Zimbabwe and further north in East Africa.

fields.Common Names: Does not have a widely used specific common name
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Gladiolus: from the Latin 'gladius', (sword), it refers to the shape of the leaves.
pretoriensis: from Pretoria.
fields.Description:
A slender perennial herb with a single leaf coming from the base, 400-500 mm long and 1-2 mm across.
The inflorescence is slender, about 400-500 mm long and it carries from 4 to 8 pink to pinkish mauve flowers about 10 mm wide and 12-15mm from top to bottom.  The lower "petal" often has a whitish blotch and some darker purplish markings, while the other "petals" have a dark purple midrib.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the Kruin Park Nature reserve and probably to other grassland reserves in Pretoria. 
Occurs in parts of North West and Gauteng.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Glandularia: from the Latin ‘glandulae’ (glands) – having glands
aristigera: having “awns”, bristle-like appendages.
fields.Description:
A trailing herbaceous perennial with mauve, purple, deep pink and occasionally white flowers. The stems are four-sided.
The leaves are in opposite pairs, ±25-30 mm and are so deeply divided that the somewhat triangular outline is not clear.
Initially the flower stems are ±20 mm long but they elongate after the flowers have dropped and the fruits develop.
fields.Notes:
An Invasive (category not clear).  It is common in grassland; also on road sides and disturbed areas.
Native to the Americas.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Gnidia: named after an Ancient Greek city located in modern-day Turkey.
capitata: forming a dense cluster of flowers.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb ±250-450 mm tall, that sprouts in the spring.  The slender stems branch above the ground.
The leaves are sessile (without a leaf stem), grey-green, narrow (±30 x 3-6 mm), and they have a sharp tip.
The flower heads can have up to 15 individual flowers and the flowers are trumpet-shaped ±15-20mm long opening up to five pointed petals.  They are mustard yellow and covered with fine silky hairs.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to wetland reserves including Colbyn Valley.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Free State.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Gomphocarpus: from the Greek 'gomphos' (a club), and 'karpos' (fruit).
fruticosus: meaning shrubby.
fields.Description:
An upright shrub, ±800mm to 2 metres tall and branching at the top to make a crown.  The stems and leaves contain a poisonous milky sap.  The long, narrow leaves are in opposite pairs.
Three to ten flowers about 10mm across, are carried in pendulous clusters.  They are white to cream-coloured, sometimes with some pink in the centre.  Each flower has a calyx of 5 white recurved sepals and 5 waxy petals that are fused together.  Each petal has a pouch-like projection and the petals and their pouches form a crown-like structure called a corona.
Each fruit is a slender egg-shaped and slightly curved balloon covered in soft spines or bristles up to 10 mm long and with a sharp-pointed “beak” at one end. They turn brown with age, and split open at maturity to release their numerous seeds.
fields.Notes:
It is widespread in South Africa, often occurring in abandoned farmlands.
Native to Africa as far north as Ethiopia and Somalia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Gomphocarpus: from the Greek 'gomphos' (a club), and 'karpos' (fruit).
physocarpus: from the Greek 'physa' (bladder) and 'karpos', fruit
fields.Description:
An introduced weed that is very similar to Gomphocarpus fruticosus and easily confused, but the FRUITS ARE DIFFERENT.
The fruits are inflated like a balloon, almost spherical, often with a slight indentation at the other end and they have characteristic soft spines. 
The leaves are often slightly broader that those of G. fruticosus
fields.Notes: Indigenous to Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape and Western Cape.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Gomphrena:  one source suggest it’s from the Ancient Greek γόμφος (gompros, "peg")
celosioides: like a Celosia.
fields.Description:
A prostrate much-branched herbaceous perennial, often forming a mat. 
The leaves are in opposite pairs, ±15 long and 5 mm wide, hairless on top but with long hairs underneath and on the margins of the leaves.
The inflorescence is at the end of the stem, more or less spherical and ±10-12 mm across, but becoming longer.
The flowers are a pale greenish white with yellow stamens protruding.
fields.Notes:
A common WEED in our reserves.
Native to South America, it has become naturalised in Africa, Asia, Australia and many countries in the Pacific.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Graderia: named by the English botanist, George Bentham, an anagram of another plant Gerardia.
 subintegra: almost entire.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb with sometimes erect and sometimes trailing shoots.
The stems are square in cross-section.
The leaves are sessile (i.e. with no leaf stalk) alternate and hairy.
The flowers are mostly pink, occasionally a deep lilac pink and occasionally white.  All the shades are present in Kruin Park.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Kruin Park and other reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.  Also occurs in Swaziland.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Grewia: named after Nehemiah Grew, an English physician.
occidentalis: from 'occidens" meaning west.
fields.Description:
A scrambling deciduous shrub or small tree up to 2-3m high.
The leaves are alternate and simple with three distinct veins from the base. They are shiny deep green and may be slightly hairy on both surfaces. They are usually held in a horizontal plane towards the light.
The pink to purple, star-shaped flowers (±20-30 mm) appear in summer 
The fruits are very distinctive having four lobes although fruits with fewer lobes are common.  They turn dark red to reddish-brown in the autumn.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several of Pretoria's reserves.
Occurs in all 9 provinces of South Africa.  Also native to Zimbabwe and Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Guilleminea: named after the French botanist Jean Baptiste Antoine Guillemin.
densa: meaning dense.
fields.Description:
A woolly, prostrate mat-forming perennial herb, with hairy stems. 
The leaves are in opposite pairs, egg-shaped with a point at the apex, ± 10 x 6 mm, hairless on the upper surface but with long matted white hairs on the lower surface.
The flowers are tiny ± 3 mm, 5-pointed, whitish bells, in dense clusters close to the leaves.
fields.Notes:
A common WEED in the reserves in Pretoria.
Native to tropical South America, Central America and the southern United States; it is a widespread weed in tropical and warm temperate zones.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Gymnosporia: from the Greek 'gymnos' (naked) and 'sporia' (seed).
heterophylla: (different or variable leaves).
fields.Description:
A deciduous and sometimes semi-deciduous shrub or small tree of 2-4 metres.
The young stems are heavily armed with long straight spines and are dark reddish brown but the older stems are dark grey-brown.
The leaves are on short stalks, leathery and darkish green, ±70 mm long and 10 mm wide with rounded tips.
The small flowers are in dense clusters along the branches in late summer.
The fruit is a capsule with three segments.
fields.Notes:
Native, ie indigenous to some of Pretoria's reserves.
Widespread in much of South Africa.  It occurs in Africa as far north as Ethiopia and Sudan.

fields.Scientific Name: Gymnosporia polyacanthus subsp. vaccinifolia, previously Maytenus polyacantha subsp. vaccinifolia
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Gymnosporia: from the Greek 'gymnos' (naked) and 'sporia' (seed).
polyacanthus: many thorns.
vaccinifolia: with leaves like those of the plant Vaccinium.
fields.Description:
A dense evergreen shrub up to about 1 metre high.
The branches a very spiny with straight spines.
The leaves are leathery, dark green, linear and rounded at the ends. 
The white flowers are clustered along the branches.
The fruits are yellowish capsules that turn brownish-red when ripe, roundish with three segments, and they break open at maturity to release seeds.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves in Pretoria.
Endemic (i.e. exclusive) to South Africa.  Native to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Gymnosporia: from the Greek 'gymnos' (naked) and 'sporia' (seed).
tenuispina: 'tenuis' (slender), 'spina' (thorns).
fields.Description:
A deciduous shrub with many stems. The branchlets are often reddish.
The leaves are light green, shallowly toothed and ±70 mm long and 10 mm wide.
The fruits are bell-shaped and are initially green becoming yellowish to brick red.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Free State.  It is also native to Eastern Botswana .

fields.Common Names: The common name is not appropriate
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Helichrysum: from the Greek 'helios' (sun) and 'chrysos' (gold).
miconiifolium: leaves similar to the plant Miconia.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb up to 500 mm high.
The leaves are almost hairless, lance-shaped, up to 100 mm long and strongly veined below.
The flower stems are usually unbranched, erect and slightly woolly. 
The Inflorescence is a terminal, flattish, compact cluster of "flowers", with several branches all springing from about same point.
The flowers are cream coloured or yellow.
The seed head consists of many seeds, each with a  stiff hair-like structure, called a pappus, attached to the top.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in much of eastern South Africa and further north.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Helichrysum: from the Greek 'helios' (sun) and 'chrysos' (gold).
rugulosum: meaning wrinkled
fields.Description:
A small perennial herb with many upright stems up to 250 mm high.
The white felted stems are densely covered with greyish-green linear leaves that are white felted on the reverse.
The compact flower-heads are pink at the start but soon become creamy.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape and the eastern part of Western Cape.  Also found beyond our borders.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Helichrysum: from the Greek 'helios' (sun) and 'chrysos' (gold).
fields.Description:
A scrambling herb up to 800 mm high.
The stems are ribbed or with continuous wings and are thickly felted. 
The leaves are long and narrow, ± 50-100 mm long with the margins rolled under, covered with whitish felt  and wrapped around the stem.
The dense, ± 50-100 mm flower head is flat-topped, with branches that arise at different points but that reach about the same height.  The florets are yellow.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.  It's range extends to Africa south of the Sahara and also to Yemen.

fields.Family: BORAGINACEAE, the Borage and Forget-me-not family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Heliotropium: Ἥλιος (helios) is Greek for "sun", and τρέπειν (trepein) "to turn" referring to a notion that the flowers turned to face the sun.
amplexicaule: clasping the stem, referring to the leaves.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb ±150-300 mm tall, with creeping, branched stems that radiate outwards from a woody rootstock. 
The leaves are alternately arranged, ±40-80 mm long, roughly hairy, with wavy margins and they clasp the stem.
The flowers are in terminal heads of several curved, one-sided spikes.  They are mauve to purple with an orange throat.
fields.Notes:
A common WEED in Pretoria's reserves.
Native to South America, it has become naturalised in warm temperate and tropical regions.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Hermannia: named after Prof. Paul Herman, a German professor of botany at Leyden and one of the first travellers and collectors at the Cape.
fields.Description:
A small prostrate herb.
It's leaves are usually reddish-brown, roughly oval, with wavy, sometimes slightly toothed margins and with prominent veins.
The tiny, drooping, bell-shaped flowers are on upright stems and are orange, pinkish, yellow or creamy white.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Colbyn Valley, Kruin Park and probably other reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape, also in parts of Northern Cape and Western Cape.  Its range includes Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Heteropogon: hetero (variable) pogon (beard) 
contortus: meaning tangled or twisted.
fields.Description:
A perennial tuft grass.  
The leaves and stems are green sometimes bluish-green and usually hairless.
The seed heads arise singly or in pairs from the axils of the upper leaves. 
The spikelets are paired, one female and the other male. 
The fertile spikelet bears a bristle-like awn which may cling to one's clothes and which intertwine at maturity.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to many reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in all of South Africa, southern Africa, southern Asia, Oceania and northern Australia.
The basic unit of the inflorescence (flower-stem) of grasses is the spikelet, which is the sub-unit of a spike.  The spike is generally surrounded by scaly bracts called glumes (which are the husks of cereal crops).

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Hibiscus: from the Ancient Greek 'ibískos' for the plant known as White Mallow (Althaea).
aethiopicus: of Ethiopia, a historic name for large parts of Africa.
ovatus: referring to the leaf shape.
fields.Description:
A small herbaceous perennial.  The stems are covered with bristly hairs. 
The leaves are variable, simple or 3-lobed with a blunt tip and their margins are also bristly.
The flowers are solitary in the leaf axils, usually yellow sometimes pink or turning pink with age.  The stigmas are bright red.
The fruit is a flattened capsule.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Colbyn Valley.
Occurs in much of South Africa except the driest parts.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Hibiscus: from the Ancient Greek 'ibískos' for the plant known as White Mallow (Althaea).
fields.Description:
A perennial herb up to 2 m high.  Older stems become woody stems.
The light green heart-shaped leaves are toothed and have a long leaf stem and soft velvety hairs.
The flowers appear in late summer and are lemon-yellow, up to 100 mm, with a deep brick red to maroon centre.
The epicalyx persists as the flattish fruit develops.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Eugene Marais Park.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.
It is also native to tropical East Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Hilliardiella: in honour of Dr Olive May Hilliard who studied Asteraceae in KwaZulu-Natal.
aristata: means with a beard or awned.
fields.Description:
An upright herbaceous perennial ±400 mm tall covered in silvery silky hairs. 
It dies down in winter and produces new growth in spring.
The leaves are long and narrow ±30-45 mm long and they have no stalk.
The inflorescence (flower head) has no outer ray florets, it has only disc florets with tiny pointed petals that give it a frilly appearance.  These appear in spring to early summer
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape.  Also native to Africa beyond our boundaries.

fields.Scientific Name: Hilliardiella aristata white form (previously Vernonia aristata)
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Hilliardiella: in honour of Dr Olive May Hilliard who studied Asteraceae in KwaZulu-Natal.
aristata: means with a beard or awned.
fields.Description:
An upright herbaceous perennial ±400 mm tall covered in silvery silky hairs. 
It dies down in winter and produces new growth in spring.
The leaves are long and narrow ±30-45 mm long and they have no stalk.
The inflorescence (flower head) has no outer ray florets, it has only disc florets with tiny pointed petals that give it a frilly appearance.  These appear in spring to early summer
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Kruin Park.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape.  Also native to Africa beyond our boundaries.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Hypochaeris:  from the Greek ὑπό (ypo) meaning ‘under’ and and χοῖρος (choiros) meaning ‘pig’
radicata: from the Latin radico (to take root)
fields.Description:
A perennial herb that regrows every spring from a thickened rootstock to form a flat rosette.  
The leaves are ±30-200 mm long, 5-50 mm wide, lobed and covered in fine hairs.
Forked stems carry bright yellow composite flower heads typical of the Daisy family.  (Stems of the very similar Dandelion, Taraxacum officinale, are hollow and never forked.)
Each individual flower is followed by a small brown seed with a white feathery 'parachute'.
fields.Notes:
A common WEED in Kruin Park.
Native to Europe, it has become naturalised in many parts of the world.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Hypoestes: from the Greek. ‘hypo’ (beneath) and ‘estia’ (house) referring to the way the leaf-like bracts cover the calyx. 
forskaolii: named after Pehr Forsskål, a Finnish-born student of Linnaeus.
fields.Description:
A shade-loving, perennial herb often sprawling, ±150-300 mm tall. Although it is taller and evergreen is moist situations, it tends to die down in winter. 
The leaves are opposite and on a short leaf stem, ±25-60x12-25 mm, and covered in short hairs. 
The flowers are in clusters, held in hairy bracts at the tips of the branches and in the axils of the leaves. They are 2-lipped and are white to pale pinkish with dark lilac markings.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.  
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape and Western Cape.
Widespread in tropical and Southern Africa. Also in Saharan Highlands, Arabia and Madagascar.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Hypoestes: from the Greek ὑπό ‘hypo’ (beneath) and ‘estia’ (house) referring to the way the leaf-like bracts cover the calyx. 
phyllostachya from the Greek phyllon (leaf) and stachys (ear of grain) a reference to the presence of leaf-like bracts on the flowering shoots.
fields.Description:
An evergreen perennial herb, ±75-150 mm tall 
Its leaves are egg-shaped but with a pointed apex. They are dark green with pink or lavender spots.
The flowers appear sporadically in summer, are tiny and are held on spikes up to 150mm long.
fields.Notes:
Native to Madagascar.
INTRODUCED to Kruin Park, probably with dumped garden refuse.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Hypoxis: from the Greek words ‘hypo’ (below) and oxy (sharp or pointed) referring to the pointed base of the fruit. 
argentea: means silvery, a reference to the silvery hairs mainly on the reverse of the leaves.
fields.Description:
A small, ±20-60 mm tall, herbaceous perennial.  
In spring, leaves grow from the quite large underground stem base into three rows that radiate slightly outwards.  The leaves are narrow, ±2-7 mm wide and they are folded into a V-shape.  They die back in winter.
The yellow star-shaped flowers are 12 mm across and have 6 petals.
The fruit is a capsule that splits across its diameter to release the ripe black seeds.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Kruin Park where I found only one small plant; also Colbyn Valley.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape and Western Cape.
Also occurs beyond our borders.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Hypoxis: from the Greek 'hypo' (below) and 'oxy' a combining form meaning sharp or pointed, referring to the pointed base of the ovary or fruit.
rigidula: referring to the somewhat stiff leaves.
fields.Description:
The leaves are upright and long (±400-800 mm and in some situations taller). They are U-shaped in cross-section. One subspecies is densely hairy the other is much less hairy. The leaves appear with the flowers after the first summer rains and they die down in winter. The leaf bases are enclosed in a sheath. 
The flowers are symmetrical with 6 tepals and are bright yellow.
The fruit is a capsule that splits across its diameter to expose the small black seeds.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Colbyn Valley, Kruin Park.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape and Northern Cape, 
Not endemic to South Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Imperata: meaning imperial, (The reference to the plant is not clear).
cylindrica: cylinder-like probably referring to the shape of the flower spike.
fields.Description:
A wetland grass, spreading with long rhizomes and often forming dense stands.
The inflorescences are silvery and narrow when young, opening up into broad cottonwool spikes later.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Colbyn Valley.
Occurs mainly in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, eastern Free State and to an extent in the western provinces of South Africa.  It is native to much of Africa, South-east Asia.
The basic unit of the inflorescence (flower-stem) of grasses is the spikelet, which is the sub-unit of a spike.  The spike is generally surrounded by scaly bracts called glumes (which are the husks of cereal crops).

fields.Common Names: Does not have a widely recognized or distinct widespread common name in English or Afrikaans, plants in the genus Indigofera are often referred to as Wild Indigo
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Indigofera: meaning Indigo-bearing (Indigofera tinctoria was one of the original sources of indigo dye).
cryptantha: meaning inconspicuous flowers.
fields.Description:
A small shrub with several stems up to 400 mm high.  
The ±50-80 mm long leaves are crowded on the stems and hairless.  They have 8-12 opposite pairs of leaflets and they lack the glands that some species of Indigofera have. 
The flower stems are short, carried in the axils of the leaves and somewhat concealed among the leaves.  The flowers are small and pinkish.
The fruit is a sickle-shaped pod deeply constricted between each seed.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.  
Occurs in all of South Africa except in the Western Cape.  Also native to Namibia, Botswana and Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Indigofera: meaning Indigo-bearing (Indigofera tinctoria was one of the original sources of indigo dye).
hedyantha: 'hedy' meaning sweet and 'anthos' flower.
fields.Description:
A small shrub sometimes as high as 300 mm
The leaves are compound with 2-4 opposite pairs of greyish-green leaflets that are folded upward along the midrib.
The buds are covered with very short brown hairs, which remain on the reverse of the standard (the upper petal).
The flowers appear in spring and early summer and are dark pinkish-red with a darker red centre.
The pods are cylindrical.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.  
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Indigofera: meaning Indigo-bearing (Indigofera tinctoria was one of the original sources of indigo dye).
zeyheri: in honour of K.L.P. Zeyher, a German botanist who was active in South Africa in the early 19th century.
fields.Description:
A slender sprawling perennial herb up to 500 mm wide.
The leaves are compound with 5 to 7 pairs of greyish-green hairless leaflets.
The flower stems arise from the axils of the leaves and are much longer than the leaves.
The flowers are white to pinkish.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.  
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Free State.  Also common Lesotho, Swaziland and southern Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ipomoea: ips or ipos (supposedly from the Greek, a worm) ηομοιος (iomoios) = similar – hence worm-like possibly referring to its twining stems.
cairica: from Cairo, where this species was first collected.
fields.Description:
A vigorous, perennial climber, growing up to about 5 metres, with smooth twining branches. 
The leaves are green, ±30-100 mm across, palmate (like spread out fingers).
The flowers appear throughout the year and are trumpet-shaped, ±30-60 mm long and ±40-60 mm in diameter, purple to pinkish with a dark eye.  They close in mid-afternoon. 
The fruit is a roundish capsule (like a pod with more than one compartment), ±8-12 mm in diameter initially green turning brown before they rupture releasing hairy seeds.
fields.Notes:
Not a listed invasive but it is a troublesome WEED
Ipomoea cairica is indigenous throughout tropical Africa, and from the eastern Mediterranean through parts of Asia to Taiwan. It has naturalised in many countries.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ipomoea: ips or ipos (supposedly from the Greek, a worm) ηομοιος (iomoios) = similar – hence worm-like possibly referring to its twining stems.
indica: means from India, but I. indica is native to the New World so the name almost certainly refers to the West Indies.
fields.Description:
A vigorous trailing or climbing vine, with hairy stems. It is a perennial but it cannot survive below 7 °C.
Its leaves are ±50-90 mm long and 35-70mm wide, mostly 3-lobed and occasionally heart-shaped.
Its flowers are larger than I. purpurea, ±60-70 mm across blue to purple and the petals are fused into a trumpet shape.  White, to pink and reddish hybrids occur.
fields.Notes:
Not a listed invasive but it is a troublesome WEED.
Native of the Caribbean, Central and South America, but widely naturalised in the tropics and warm temperate areas.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ipomoea: ips or ipos (supposedly from the Greek, a worm) ηομοιος (iomoios) = similar – hence worm-like possibly referring to its twining stems.
obscura: indistinct, obscure.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb with trailing or twining stems up to 3 m long, growing from a narrow taproot. 
The leaves are heart-shaped with a wavy margin and a pointed apex, 25-75 mm long, and downy with soft short hairs on both surfaces.  The leaf stem is long.
The flowers are trumpet-shaped and usually yellow.
The fruit is a spherical capsule, tipped with the persistent style base.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.  
Occurs mainly in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Free State also in the eastern parts of Eastern Cape and Northern Cape.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ipomoea: ips or ipos (supposedly from the Greek, a worm) ηομοιος (iomoios) = similar – hence worm-like possibly referring to its twining stems.
purpurea: from the Latin meaning purple.
fields.Description:
A fast growing, trailing or climbing annual. 
The leaves have hairy stalks, and they are heart-shaped with a pointed tip, with some with short, soft hairs above and below.
The flowers are mostly solitary.  The calyx has bristly hairs.  The petals are fused into a trumpet shape, generally purplish blue with a reddish star but may be white, pink, blue or magenta; the tube is white or paler below. 
The fruit is a spherical, hairless capsule (like a pod with more than one compartment). The seeds are black.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE.
Indigenous to South America; widely naturalised in the tropics.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ipomoea: ips or ipos (supposedly from the Greek, a worm) ηομοιος (iomoios) = similar – hence worm-like possibly referring to its twining stems.
purpurea: from the Latin meaning purple.
fields.Description:
A fast growing, trailing or climbing annual. 
The leaves have hairy stalks, and they are heart-shaped with a pointed tip, with some with short, soft hairs above and below.
The flowers are mostly solitary.  The calyx has bristly hairs.  The petals are fused into a trumpet shape, generally purplish blue with a reddish star but may be white, pink, blue or magenta; the tube is white or paler below. 
The fruit is a spherical, hairless capsule (like a pod with more than one compartment). The seeds are black.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE.
Indigenous to South America; widely naturalised in the tropics.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Jacaranda: from the South American Tupi name for the tree,  'jakara'na'.
mimosifolia: leaves lika a Mimosa.
fields.Description:
A very well-known tree in Pretoria.
Some people confuse young plants in the reserve with the Common Hook-thorn, Senegalia caffra.
Jacaranda has large, bipinnately compound leaves (the leaflets are not carried on the main "stem" of the leaf), the leaves are in opposite pairs and Jacaranda has no thorns.
fields.Notes:
Not listed as invasive in Gauteng but it is troublesome in a nature reserve.
CONTROL:  Cut the plants down to just above the ground and paint the stump immediately with Kaput.  Don't use excessive amounts of Kaput and be careful not to spill it or get it straight onto the soil.
Old trees that have been cut down and not treated need repeated treatment.
TARGET SPRAY regrowth to avoid spraying other plants, using one of about 10 herbicides containing Triclopyr.
Native to South America

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Jasminum: the Latinised form of the Persian name, yasmin. 
multipartitum: from the Latin meaning 'with many parts or compartments'.
fields.Description:
This is a large, scrambling, mostly evergreen shrub, reaching a height of ±1.5 to 2 metres.
The leaves are bright green, in opposite pairs, ±30-45 mm long and 12-20 mm wide with a pointed tip.
The closed flower buds are pink- to reddish. The flower petals are fused at the base and the ±30 mm long tube is dark pink.  The five-petalled, white flowers are ±30-45 mm across, and they appear in masses from early spring to summer. They have a delicate perfume during the day that becomes stronger in the evening. 
The fruit is a berry (like a tomato) often twin berries from. Initially they are green but they turn to a shiny, bluish-black when ripe.
fields.Notes:
Not indigenous to the reserves of Pretoria, INTRODUCED. 
Native to Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape and Limpopo.
Also indigenous to Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Swaziland.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Jasminum: the Latinised form of the Persian name, yasmin. 
nudiflorum: meaning naked flower.
fields.Description:
A deciduous shrub ±1.5 to 2 metres tall with long, arching branches. 
The leaves are in opposite pairs and each leaf has three leaflets.
The ±25mm wide flowers are bright yellow and appear on the bare branches in early spring.
fields.Notes:
Not indigenous to the reserves of Pretoria, where it occurs it has been INTRODUCED. 
Native to northern China

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Kalanchoe: from a Sinitic source akin to Cantonese 'Qiélán cài' which apparently means galaxy literally “temple plant".
beharensis: is in reference to the occurrence of this plant at Behara, a town in Madagascar
fields.Description:
An evergreen shrub, ±1-2 metres tall.  The stem is succulent and unbranched becoming hard and displaying large leaf scars where the leaves have dropped off.
The fleshy leaves are olive green to grey-green, in opposite pairs, triangular, usually downy (covered with short, soft hairs), and irregularly lobed and crimped at the edges, 80-400 mm long and 70-350 mm wide.  K. beharensis may reproduce asexually by producing plantlets on leaf margins, which when distributed on a suitable substrate will form new plants.
The inflorescences appear in spring to summer, they are many-flowered, large ±200-400 mm high, forming a branched head. 
The urn-shaped individual flowers are on short stalks, and are ±7 mm long and across. Blooming occurs from spring to summer, and flowers are small and yellowish to pinkish.
fields.Notes:
Not native to the Pretoria area.
Indigenous to Madagascar.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Kalanchoe: from a Sinitic source akin to Cantonese 'Qiélán cài' which apparently means galaxy literally “temple plant".
paniculata: referring to the way that the flowers are carried on branches of the main axis.
fields.Description:
A succulent shrublet that sends up a tall flower stem in early summer until it is ± 500-600 mm high.  It flowers in the autumn.
The leaves are fleshy, untoothed, green to yellowish-green and are covered with a fine whitish bloom (a waxy powder that is easily removed by rubbing).
The lower leaves have no petiole (leaf stem) and they form a rosette, while the upper leaves do have a petiole and are in pairs.  Older leaves may be edged with reddish brown.
The inflorescence is flat-topped and is made up of many flowers.
The calyx (outer whorl) is elongated and green and four yellow petals protrude at the end.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.  
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape, Free State and Northern Cape.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Kalanchoe: from a Sinitic source akin to Cantonese 'Qiélán cài' which apparently means galaxy literally “temple plant".
rotundifolia: rounded leaves.
fields.Description:
A succulent with rounded leaves that are carried at the lower part on a slender stem.  The leaves are not as round as the name rotundifolia suggests.
The flowers are borne in the autumn in a flat-topped inflorescence with a long erect stalk tubular flower. The flower buds are pinkish orange, and the flowers are tubular with dark yellow to orange petals at the tip.  The flowers turn reddish and twisted as they age.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.  
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape and Northern Cape.
Also native to Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Swaziland and Tanzania.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Kalanchoe: from a Sinitic source akin to Cantonese 'Qiélán cài' which apparently means galaxy literally “temple plant".
sexangularis: this suggests that its stems have six angles (angularis). In fact it has square stems.
fields.Description:
This succulent shrublet is very similar to Kalanchoe paniculata.
The differences are that the leaves of Kalanchoe sexangularis have lobed margins and that they are  often reddish.
fields.Notes:
NOT native to Pretoria reserves.
In Kruin Park it has spread from a small patch in 2003 to the extent that it threatens the habitat of other native plants including Kalanchoe paniculata.  It is vital that we control its spread in the reserve.
It is indigenous to the eastern escarpment of Limpopo and Mpumalanga and in KwaZulu-Natal.  It is also native to Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Swaziland.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Kalanchoe: from a Sinitic source akin to Cantonese 'Qiélán cài' which apparently means galaxy literally “temple plant".
thyrsiflora: refers to the way that the flowers are carried on branches of the main axis.
fields.Description:
A succulent perennial, its stalkless leaves are large, ±100-120 mm long, greyish-green edged in red and coated with a white powdery bloom.  They form an upright rosette.
The flowering stem is tall, up to 1000 mm, it is silvery in colour and the leaves are smaller. 
The inflorescence is a thyrse (that is a flower cluster with a central spike that has side branches also clustered with flowers) and the tubular greenish-yellow flowers with yellow recurved tips are densely packed along the central spike.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.  
Occurs in Limpopo, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape.  Also Lesotho and Swaziland.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Karomia: named after Kà Rôm in Vietnam where the first species of the genus Karomia was found. 
speciosa: Latin for splendid or showy.
fields.Description:
A shrub up to ±1-2 metres tall.  The branches have smooth greyish-brown bark.
The leaf stems are ±7 mm long and the leaves are downy (with soft short hairs) and have coarsely toothed margins.  They are darker green above and paler green below. 
The calyx is like a Chinese hat and dusty-pink or mauve in colour.
The flower is deep-blue or violet and it has a 10-15 mm long, tube that bends downwards.  The open flower has two lips.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to Kruin Park.
Not native to the Pretoria area.
Indigenous to Limpopo, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal
Also occurs in Mozambique (Maputo province), Swaziland, north into tropical Africa and Madagascar.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Kiggelaria: named after Frans Kiggelaer, a Dutch botanist and curator of a garden in Leiden in the late 17th century.
africana: from Africa
fields.Description:
A small to medium-sized tree, up to ±4 or 5 metres tall in Kruin Park.  It has pale grey bark that becomes rough on older branches.
The leaves are vaguely reminiscent of those of a peach, mid- to dark green and paler underneath. 
The flowers appear in spring to early summer.  They are small, ±3 mm across, pale yellowish green, and unisexual, with the sexes on different trees. The female flowers are solitary, while the male flowers are in sparsely branched heads. 
The fruit is a spherical, yellowish-green capsule, covered with rough, warty yellowish green growths.  The capsule splits in late summer into five compartments revealing black seeds with a sticky orange-red coating.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to Kruin Park (planted by the Parks Department in about 2002 at the request of a Kruin Street resident).
It is native to much of South Africa often in forests, along streams and rivers and sometimes in drier situations.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Kirkia: named after Dr (later Sir) John Kirk, an English doctor and a plant collector, who accompanied Livingstone on his Zambezi expedition.
wilmsii: named after Friedrich Wilms, a German apothecary and botanical collector.
fields.Description:
A small to medium-sized tree, up to ±4 or 5 metres tall in Kruin Park.  It has smooth grey bark.  The smaller branches have conspicuous leaf scars.
The leaves are crowded at the ends of the branches.  They are arranged alternatively on the branches and have 10 to 15 opposite pairs of glossy dark green leaflets ±30 mm long and 12 mm wide and a terminal leaflet.  The leaves turn reddish to a beautiful bright red in the autumn.
The flowers are small, ±3 mm across, pale green, and in dense flower heads that are on long stalks in the axils of the leaves. 
The fruit is a narrowly oval green capsule that turns brown.  It splits into 4 compartments that remain attached at the apex.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to Kruin Park (a single plant was almost certainly planted near to Kruin Street), it is tending to spread from seed dropped by the adult tree.
It is native to parts of Limpopo and Mpumalanga and endemic to South Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Lactuca: from the Latin 'latteus', (milky or full of milk) referring to the milky sap in the plant. The Latin term 'Lactuca' also means lettuce.
inermis: unarmed, with no spines.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb that grows to ±100-300 mm but occasionally up to 1.5 m tall. 
The stems and leaves contain a milky latex. 
The green or bluish-green leaves are long and narrow, sessile (without a leaf stem), alternate, and scattered along the stem but crowded at the base.  
The flower heads have from five to many, strap-shaped ray florets and no disk florets.  They are white to pale blue or mauve, and rarely yellow.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.  
Occurs predominantly in the eastern half of South Africa but it is also native to the eastern part of Northern Cape and coastal Western Cape.
It is widely distributed in tropical Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Lactuca: from the Latin 'latteus', (milky or full of milk) referring to the milky sap in the plant. The Latin term 'Lactuca' also means lettuce.
serriola: pertaining to salad, being one form of an old name for chicory.
fields.Description:
An erect annual (sometimes biennial) herb, ±700 mm tall in Kruin Park with thorny stems.
The leaves have no leaf stem.  They are grey green, veined, ±70-100 x 20-40 mm, wider at the apex, quite deeply lobed and with fine spines on the margins.
The “flowers” have toothed, strap-shaped yellow ray florets, and no disk florets.  They appear in summer.
fields.Notes:
WEED, often on disturbed land.
Native of Eastern Mediterranean and North Africa

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Laggera: in honour of Dr. Franz Josef Lagger, a Swiss physician and botanist.
crispata: waved, curled.
fields.Description:
A sturdy much-branched herb ±1 m tall. in Kruin Park  The stems and main branches are often distinctly winged. 
The leaves are sessile (with no leaf stem), oblong, and the margins are toothed with hardened tips.  The leaf surfaces are covered with hairs that can be soft or rough to the touch. 
The flower stem is large and the flowers are carried on branches of the main stem. 
The involucre (i.e. the base of all daisy flowers) consists of tightly packed green bracts with pointed scales.  The flower head is not typical for a daisy and it has pink florets that protrude from the involucre.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.  
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.
It is ddistributed throughout tropical Africa and tropical Asia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Lannea: refers to the dense, woolly hairs on the young parts of the plants. 
discolor: from Latin, 'of different colours'.
fields.Description:
A medium-sized deciduous tree usually 3-6 metres in height with a neat rounded crown. 
The bark is thick, grey, quite rough and cracking into small blocks which peel off. 
The small, pale yellow flowers appear before the leaves and they are produced in ±80-120 mm long spikes.
The leaves are borne at the end of the branches.  They are compound with up to 5 pairs of leaflets and a terminal leaflet. The upper surface of the leaflets is green and the lower surface grey with dense felty hairs.  They turn a lovely golden yellow in the autumn.
The ±10 mm fruits are green turning purple as they ripen.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the northern Quartzitic parts of Kruin Park.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga. Also indigenous to Caprivi in Namibia, 
Botswana, Zimbabwe, Swaziland, Mozambique, Zambia and Malawi.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Lantana: from the Latin name of the wayfaring tree Viburnum lantana, the flowers of which closely resemble Lantana. 
camara: from the Greek, (arched, chambered, or vaulted).
fields.Description:
A shrub of ± 1 metre high but it can grow bigger. 
The flower heads are carried the axils of the leaves and they appear from mid-summer to autumn.
The flowers are yellow turning orange and a paler yellow turning pinkish.
Each pollinated flower produces a succulent berry-like fruit and the single seed is enclosed in a hard layer like a peach has.
The seed is dispersed widely by birds that eat the fruit.
fields.Notes:
A SERIOUS Category 1b INVASIVE.  It will often out-compete other desirable species and dramatically reduce biodiversity. 
CONTROL:  Cut the plants down to just above the ground and paint the stump immediately with Kaput.  Don't use excessive amounts of Kaput and be careful not to spill it or get it straight onto the soil.
If spraying is necessary for any reason TARGET SPRAY to avoid spraying other plants, using one of about 10 herbicides containing Triclopyr.  DO NOT SPRAY with a product containing Picloram. It is NOT appropriate in a nature area.
 Native to Central and South America.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Lantana: from the Latin name of the wayfaring tree Viburnum lantana, the flowers of which closely resemble Lantana.
rugosa: from the Latin, 'rugosus,-a,-um' (wrinkle) referring to the wrinkled leaves.
fields.Description:
A woody, sub-shrub usually 500mm high and occasionally up to 1 metre, its stems and branches are 4-angled.
The leaves have a wrinkled appearance due to the deeply recessed veins and they become rough with age.  They are opposite, 30-50mm long and 12-30mm wide, with shallowly scalloped margins; they are rounded at the base and they narrow into a wedge shape at the leaf stem.
The flower stems appear from the leaf axils, and they have broad green floral bracts between each flower.  The flowers are tubular opening up into 5 lobes and are lilac to rose pink or reddish purple with a yellow throat.
The fruit is a small 2-3 mm purple to wine-coloured drupe (like a peach with a single seed enclosed in a hard layer).
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs mainly in eastern South Africa but also extending into the eastern parts of northern Cape and western Cape.  Also native to Namibia, Angola, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Lesotho, Swaziland and Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ledebouria: named in honour of the German-Estonian botanist, Professor Carl Friedrich von Ledebour.
revoluta: meaning rolled back, used to describe the way the tepals roll back when the flowers are open.
fields.Description:
A perennial that overwinters as a bulb (like an onion with a basal stem and scales that are ±3 mm thick).  It is usually solitary although sometimes a few bulbs form a clump.
The bulb produces 3 or more flower stems, in a spike like a bottlebrush with many small, reddish purple flowers. The flower buds are purplish grey. 
The leaves appear with or after the flowers. They are long and narrow or slightly triangular, green, usually with dark spots.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to all nine provinces of South Africa, most common in the wetter, eastern parts.
Also indigenous to Africa as far north as Chat and Ethiopia and to Yemen, India and Sri Lanka.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Leo: Lion and otis: ear 
nepetifolia: leaf reminiscent of Nepeta, the Catmint
fields.Description:
An upright and sparsely branched annual herbaceous plant usually growing 1-2 m tall.
Its leaves have a longish leaf stem, they are in opposite pairs, wide at the base and tapering to a point, the have distinctly toothed margins and they are slightly hairy.
The flowers are borne in widely spaced, dense rounded clusters.  The individual flowers are orange, tubular and two-lipped and they are surrounded by a green calyx-tube.
After the flowers drop, the flower clusters form a hard, spiny ball.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria including Klapperkop and Kruin Park.
Occurs in Limpopo, Gauteng and Mpumalanga
Also native to tropical Africa and southern India

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Leucas: from the Greek 'leucos' for white.
martinicensis: unclear.
fields.Description:
An annual herb ±20-90 mm high.
The stems are usually unbranched and finely hairy or downy.
The leaves are opposite, downy, with coarsely serrated margins, up to ± 60x20 mm, and often wedge-shaped at the base.
A number of inflorescences are spaced along the upright stem in closely spaced whorls with long thistle-like calyx teeth. 
The flowers are 2-3 mm across and white.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Free State.  Also beyond our borders.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Lippia: named after Augustin Lippi, an Italian traveller and natural historian. 
javanica: This plant was identified from material collected in Java, hence the epithet javanica, meaning 'from Java'.
fields.Description:
A small shrub ±800-1000 mm high.
The stems are more or less square.
The leaves are opposite, hairy, toothed, have clear sunken veins and are folded upwards at the midrib.  They give off a lemon-like smell when crushed.
The 2mm creamy white flowers in dense clusters and on stalks appear from summer to autumn.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to many reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape.
Also in much of Africa and beyond.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Lopholaena: from the Greek 'lophos' (a crest), and 'chlaina' (a cloak) 
coriifolia: uncertain.
fields.Description:
A woody shrub, ±600 mm tall in Kruin Park. It has rough, blackish brown bark. 
The leaves have no leaf stem, they have three main veins, are leathery, hairless and grey-green. They widen from the base to a rounded tip and they have smooth, untoothed margins.
The “flowers” protrude from a green tube, they have pinkish disk florets and the ray-florets are absent. August.  White, involucral bracts persist. 
The seed head consists of a number of seeds, each with a long silky structure, called a pappus, attached to the top.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.
Also beyond our borders.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Lotononis: a combination of the two plant names 'Lotus' and 'Ononis'.
calycina: from the Greek 'kalkynos' meaning with a noticeable calyx.
fields.Description:
A prostrate perennial herb, often forming mats. 
The compound leaves have 3 leaflets, more or less egg-shaped and they have a short, sharply pointed tip.  They are hairless above and hairy below. 
The tiny flowers appear in groups of 1-3.  The standard (the broad, upper ± erect petal) and the 2 shorter side petals are bright yellow. 
The 2 front petals are fused into a boat-shaped structure called a keel. It flowers in early spring and summer.  The pods are narrow and densely hairy.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape.
Its range extends into Lesotho and parts of Namibia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Malvastrum: derived from Malva, the generic name for the Common Mallow.
coromandelianum:
fields.Description:
An annual or short-lived perennial sub-shrub, ±400-500 mm tall in Kruin Park. It is covered in rough hairs.
The leaves are ±60 mm long and 40 mm wide tapering to a sharp point; and the margins are coarsely toothed. 
The cream or pale yellow flowers appear at the top of the stems in the leaf axils.
Like Pavonia (two of which are indigenous to Kruin Park) M. coromandelianum has a calyx (outer green whorl) and an epicalyx consisting of wide bracts. 
The fruit is a small, dry capsule, enclosed by the calyx.
fields.Notes:
A category 1b INVASIVE.
It is probably indigenous to North America, but it has become a widespread weed of disturbed places and roadsides.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Melia: from the Greek ‘μελία’, the word used by Theophrastus for the Ash, which he believed had similar leaves. 
azedarach: from the French 'azédarac' which in turn is from the Persian 'āzād dirakht' (ازادرخت ) meaning 'noble tree'
fields.Description:
The adult tree has a rounded crown, and generally measures 6–9 metres tall.
The leaves are ±200-400 x 150-300 mm, and two or three times compound.  The leaflets are dark green above and lighter green below, and the margins have asymmetrical teeth pointing forward; like the cutting edge of a saw.
The small flowers are in clusters and they have five pale lilac or purple petals.
The fruit is a drupe (with a pip like a peach), marble-sized and dull yellow.  They remain on the tree all winter.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE, it is Category 3 in urban areas.  It is nevertheless a SERIOUS invasive in nature areas.
CONTROL: Cut the plants down to just above the ground and paint the stump immediately with Kaput. Don't use excessive amounts of Kaput and be careful not to spill it or get it straight onto the soil.
If spraying is necessary for any reason TARGET SPRAY to avoid spraying other plants, using one of about 10 herbicides containing Triclopyr. DO NOT SPRAY with a product containing Picloram. It is NOT appropriate in a nature area.
It is native to South and Southeast Asia, Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and parts of Australia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Melilotus: From the Greek μέλι, méli meaning honey
officinalis: refers to its use in the medicines of the past.
fields.Description:
An annual or biennial legume ±400-500 mm tall in Kruin Park. 
The stems are light green, round or slightly furrowed. 
The leaves are sparsely distributed along the stem, alternately arranged and have three leaflets.
In midsummer the upper stems produce narrow racemes of white flowers ± 50-150 mm long. Each flower has a light green calyx and has 5 white petals.
The seedpods are black to dark grey, 3-4 mm long and each pod usualy contains one yellow seeds.
fields.Notes:
A weed.
Indigenous to much of Asia and southern Europe, from France and Spain to Kazakhstan and Myanmar, and also northeastern Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
