Melinis: uncertain, possibly from the Greek melanos, meaning black (the seeds of some species are black) or from the Latin for honey
nerviglumis: referring to the veins on the bracts (the glumes).
fields.Description:
The basic unit of the inflorescence (flower-stem) of grasses is the spikelet, which is the sub-unit of a spike. The spike is generally surrounded by scaly bracts called glumes (which are the husks of cereal crops).
A perennial grass forming clumps up to ±400 mm tall
The leaves are BLUE-GREEN 
The flowers usually appear from November to late summer, they are pinkish at first fading to white. Dense, silky hairs give the panicles a 'shining' appearance.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to all of South Africa.
Also Africa south of the Sahara.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Melinis: uncertain, possibly from the Greek melanos, meaning black (the seeds of some species are black) or from the Latin for honey.
repens: creeping
fields.Description:
The basic unit of the inflorescence (flower-stem) of grasses is the spikelet, which is the sub-unit of a spike. The spike is generally surrounded by scaly bracts called glumes (which are the husks of cereal crops).
A very common perennial grass often growing on roadsides.
it is less robust that M. nerviglumis.
The leaves are GREEN.
The flowers appear in late summer and they are from reddish, to pink to white.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to much of South Africa.
Also native to much of Africa and western Asia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Menodora: from the Greek μενος 'menos', meaning force, and Δορον 'doron', meaning gift, referring to the sustenance the plants provided to the horses of Alexander von Humboldt, a Prussian naturalist when he first encountered the genus in Mexico.
africana: of Africa.
fields.Description:
Menodora africana is a small sub-shrub (i.e. it is a woody plant but it has herbaceous branches).  
The leaves have no petiole (leaf stem) and are deeply divided.  
The calyx is also divided and reddish brown and the unopened flower bud is also reddish. 
The flowers are bright yellow and they appear in spring. The fruit is a spherical two-lobed capsule.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Colbyn Valley.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, inland KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and the eastern part of Northern Cape.
It is not endemic to South Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Mirabilis: means admirable
jalapa: Jalapa is the state capital of Veracruz in México
fields.Description:
A perennial herb usually up to I metre tall.
The stems are thick and quadrangular.
The flowers open in the afternoon.  They are funnel-shaped and have five lobes.  Usually they are yellow, red, magenta, pink or white but quite often individual flowers may be blotched, splashed or spotted with different colours and flowers with different colours sometimes occur on the same plant at the same time.
fields.Notes:
A category 1b invasive. 
It is indigenous to tropical South America.

fields.Common Names: Crane's bill, Teebossie, Tee ya thaba (Sepedi)
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Monsonia: was named after Lady Anne Monson, a botanist and collector of plants and insects. 
angustifolia, is Latin meaning narrow-leaved.
fields.Description:
An annual herb ±200-300mm tall; taller in favourable conditions.  Its stems are hairy and slightly woody at the base.
The leaves are narrowly oblong with indented veins and irregularly toothed margins. 
It flowers in late summer on long flower stems and the petals are usually mauve to bluish-mauve. The calyx (the green outer whorl of a flower) is hairy and it persists after the flower petals have dropped.  
As the fruit develops, the style elongates and points upwards.  When the fruit is mature the style splits and curls, releasing the seeds.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in all nine provinces especially on the drier parts of eastern and north-eastern South Africa.
Widespread in Africa south of the Sahara and east to Somalia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Moraea: The name 'Morea' was originally given by Philip Miller to honour Robert More of Shropshire, but it was taken over by Linnaeus and changed to Moraea.
stricta: from the Latin, meaning very straight, referring to the straight leaves.
fields.Description:
A herbaceous perennial, ±200-400 mm tall. 
The delicate flowers appear at the end of the dry winter period and are pale lilac to violet-blue with orange-yellow spots (nectar guides) on the broader outer 3 tepals.
The single long, narrow leaf appears after the flowers have faded. It is cylindrical and difficult to distinguish among the surrounding grasses.
The fruit is an longish three-celled capsule.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Free State.
Also in the eastern part of Africa as far north as Eritrea.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Mystroxylon: Mystro - spoon & xylon - wood
aethiopicum: Latin for Africa
burkeanum: refers to naturalist and collector, Joseph Burke
fields.Description:
A medium-sized to large tree.
The leaves are leathery, glossy dark green underneath and paler above and are very variable in shape.
The small yellowish green flowers appear in summer and they are followed by fleshy roundish fruits that are yellowish green turning red when they ripen.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Subspecies burkeanum is limited to the highveld areas of Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga
Subsp. aethiopicum occurs in the Western and Eastern Cape, while subsp. schlechteri extends north into Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Nidorella: from the Latin 'nidor' meaning smell and '-ella' (diminutive) alluding to the strong smell these plants have.
hottentotica: possibly a reference to Hottentot, a name that is no longer acceptable for the Khoikhoi.
fields.Description:
An erect perennial herb that branches at the top. 
Its leaves are narrow slightly wavy and densely covered with whitish woolly hairs.
The flower heads are flattish.  The disc florets are densely packed  and have two lips.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, Free State and Northern Cape.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ochna: from an ancient Greek word Ochne for Wild Pear alluding to its leaves that resemble those of this pear tree.
pretoriensis: from Pretoria.
fields.Description:
A much-branched evergreen shrub up to ± 1-2 metres high. The stems and branches have a rough grey-brown bark. 
The leaves are dark green, shiny, with slightly raised veins, ± 35 mm x 10-15 mm and often widest nearer the tip. The margins have small, shallow teeth.
The sweet-smelling, yellow flowers appear before the leaves and are solitary and sometimes in pairs on the tips of short branchlets. 
The persistent sepals become wine-red. 
The fruit is a slightly elongated drupe (fleshy with a pip like a peach), green at first becoming black and shiny when mature.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.
Also in Botswana.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ochna: from an ancient Greek word Ochne for Wild Pear alluding to its leaves that resemble those of this pear tree.
pulchra: beautiful.
fields.Description:
A deciduous tree, 2 metres tall in Kruin Park, taller elsewhere.  The twigs are brittle. The bark peels off older branches to show a smooth, creamy trunk. 
The leaves are ±80 mm long and ±30 mm wide.  In spring they are light green to bronze and they turn golden brown in autumn.
The sweetly scented flowers appear in spring.
The sepals become enlarged and turn pinkish-red. 1-3 kidney-shaped, green fruits develop and as they ripen they turn black.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ocimum: from the Latin for the herb Basil.
obovatum: an obovate leaf - longer than it is wide and widest further from the stem.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb of up to 400 mm tall, it dies down in winter and regrows in spring.
The leaves are in opposite pairs ±8-15 mm but variable in shape and size.  The leaf margins are sometimes smooth and sometimes slightly hairy.
Each flower is surrounded by a tubular green to purplish calyx and the white to pale mauve flowers appear from September to February.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in the summer rainfall parts of South Africa.  Also north to tropical East Africa and parts of India

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Oenothera: possibly from the Greek οινος θηρας (oinos theras), meaning "wine seeker".
rosea: pink
fields.Description:
A much-branched perennial herb, often flowering in the first year. 
The saucer-shaped flowers are pink with white stigmas and a yellow centre.  The flowers open in the evening and stay open until late morning.
fields.Notes:
A weed.
Indigenous to northern Mexico and Texas.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Oocephala: uncertain.
staehelinoides: reminiscent of Staehelina, a thistle-like plant.
fields.Description:
A small shrublet ± 300-500 mm tall.
The stems and leaves are covered with short grey hairs.
The leaves are long and narrow ±20-40 mm x 3-4 mm, and the margins are rolled under. 
The individual flowers are long and tubular with pointed petals and they are shades of mauve, and bluish to pinkish purple.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in southern Limpopo, eastern North West, Gauteng, north-eastern Mpumalanga and Northern Free State.
ENDEMIC to South Africa (i.e. it does not occur naturally elsewhere).

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Opuntia: named after the Ancient Greek city of Opus.
ficus-indica: means Indian Fig, one of its many common names.
fields.Description:
A perennial shrub that can grow up to 3–5 m height, with thick, succulent and oblong to spoon-shaped stems called cladodes.  The cladodes are green and function as leaves. 
All members of the Cactus family have spines that are borne from specialised structures that are in fact highly reduced branches. Flowers develop on 1 to 2-year-old cladodes from early summer, they are usually yellow but may be orange or red. 
The fruits are pale green to deep red.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE.
Opuntias hybridise easily but the wild form is thought to have originated in Mexico.  It is widely cultivated for its fruits and as a fodder crop.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Opuntia: named after the Ancient Greek city of Opus.
monacantha: referring to the single spine
fields.Description:
A succulent shrub growing up to 5 m tall, its stems are succulent, shiny green and they function as leaves.  
All members of the Cactus family have spines that are borne from specialised structures that are in fact highly reduced branches. As the name Opuntia monacantha suggests the spines are single. 
The flowers are cup-shaped, ±50-75 mm across.  The outer petals are yellow with a reddish stripe and the inner petals yellow.
The fruits are reddish-purple, fleshy, pendulous, more or less conical ±50-75 mm long and 40-50 mm in diameter.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE.
It is native to Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Papaver: named by Carl von Linne = Latin for milk (his plant had milky latex).
aculeatum: aculeate (i.e. armed with prickles).
fields.Description:
A spiny upright annual herb.
The leaves are spiny. Lower leaves have a leaf stem but higher up they have no leaf stem. The leaf margins of the leaves are usually deeply lobed.
The long flower stems are upright but bent at the top while the plant is in bud.  They straighten as the flowers open.
The fruit is a capsule with a flattened top.  When the seeds ripen the top reveals pores through which the seeds escape.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Rietvlei and possibly other reserves in Pretoria.
Mainly indigenous to the eastern part of South Africa but it also occurs in the Northern and Western Cape.
Its range includes Namibia, Lesotho and Swaziland.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Pappea: after German physician and plant collector Carl Pappe, 
capensis:  southern Africa (literally from the Cape).
fields.Description:
An evergreen tree with a height of 2-3 metres in Kruin Park.
The leaves are oblong and hard-textured ±25x120mm. 
Young plants have sharply toothed margins but the leaves of mature trees are usually untoothed. 
The flowers are borne on pendulous catkins in the axils of the leaves.
The fruits are spherical, green and velvety.  These split open to reveal bright red flesh.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape and Northern Cape.
Also northwards to eastern tropical Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Pavetta: possibly from pawatta, the Sinhalese (Sri Lankan) name for a plant in the genus.
lanceolata:  like a lance or spear head, longer than it is broad and broader at the base.
fields.Description:
An evergreen shrub, ±1-2 metres tall in Kruin Park.
The leaves are ±50 x 15 mm, usually narrower at the tip but sometimes narrower at the base; quite often with a sharp point. 
The flowers are tubular at the base opening into four petals and with prominent stamens.
The fruit is a drupe (fleshy with a pip, like a peach). Initially it is green, it turns black when it ripens.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, and Eastern Cape.
Also occurs in southern Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Pavonia: after Spanish botanist José Antonio Pavón Jiménez
burchellii: after William John Burchell, a naturalist
fields.Description:
A shrubby herb, usually up to 500 mm.
The whole plant is covered with short soft hairs.
The petiole (leaf stem) can be between 1 and 5 mm long.
The leaves are almost round to broadly egg-shaped but lobed and toothed and the veins are palmate (radiating out from a central point at the petiole).
The flowers are usually yellow, and solitary in the leaf axils (the upper angle between the petiole and the stem).
Like P. transvaalensis, P. burchellii has a calyx (outer green whorl) and an epicalyx consisting of 4-8 wide bracts joined at the base. 
The fruit is a small, dry capsule, enclosed by the calyx.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Kruin Park.
Occurs in all of South Africa except Western Cape.  Also occurs further north to East Africa and Cameroon.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Pavonia: after Spanish botanist José Antonio Pavón Jiménez.
transvaalensis: from the Transvaal.
fields.Description:
An attractive perennial herb, usually 300-500mm high.
The leaves have a stalk, and are deeply divided into 3-5 toothed lobes.
 The green calyx (outer whorl of the flower) is surrounded by an outer epicalyx that has 9 or more long narrow fringed segments that persist as the flower ages and the fruit develops.
The flowers are light greenish yellow.
The fruit is a small, dry capsule, enclosed by the calyx and the attractive epicalyx.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs mainly in Northern Gauteng and Southern 
Limpopo. Also occurs in parts of North West and Northern Mpumalanga generally closest to Northern Gauteng.
(Listed in Kirby, G. (2013). Wild Flowers of Southeast Botswana Struik Nature, Cape Town).

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Pearsonia; to honour Dr. H.H.W. Pearson, first director of Kirstenbosch National Botanic Garden.
sessilifolia: sessile leaves (with no leaf stem).
fields.Description:
A small perennial, 300-500 mm tall, it has slender hairy stems. 
The leaves are trifoliate, usually with silvery-grey surface hairs and no leaf stem.
The pea-like flowers appear mostly in spring and are clustered together at the top of branches. The petals are yellow, turning orange when pollinated. 
The pods are narrow and oblong, with silvery hairs.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.
Also native to Lesotho, Swaziland, Zimbabwe and Mozambique.
Pearsonia sessilifolia is a very variable species and currently four subspecies are recognised.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Pellaea: from the Greek word pellos, dark (most of the species of Pellaea have dark stalks).
calomelanos: calos means beautiful and melanos means black.
fields.Description:
Ferns produce spores not seeds; the spores are carried in a structure called a sorus.  
The fronds of Pellaea are carried on strong, shining black stems that are up to 200 mm long and hairless.
The rigid, blue-green leaflets have three lobes and are up to 15 mm long and wide.  
The sori of Pellaea are dark brown and they are arranged along the edges of the leaflets.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
It is common in Gauteng and occurs in the eastern half of South Africa.
Also indigenous to the eastern parts of Africa as far north as Somalia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Pennisetum: from the Latin meaning a feather, a plume, a bristle, referring to the conspicuous bristles on many species of Pennisetum.
clandestinum: hidden (the flower stems are very short and "hidden" amongst the leaves).
fields.Description: A widely used lawn grass with matted roots with underground stems known as rhizomes.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b invasive in protected areas.
CONTROL: Because it is a monocotyledon (commonly referred to as monocot) it cannot be controlled with the usually selective herbicides. TARGET spray with Glyphosate.
Indigenous to the lower altitude parts of Kenya.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Pennisetum: from the Latin meaning a feather, a plume or a bristle, referring to the conspicuous bristles on many species of Pennisetum
setaceum: also a reference to the conspicuous bristles.
fields.Description:
A perennial grass of ±500 mm that forms separate tussocks (tufts) and not runners.
Its feathery spike-like inflorescences are ±100-200 mm long, on bare stems and carried above the leaves.  It is usually purple or rose pink-coloured, fading with age.
fields.Notes:
A Category 1b INVASIVE, it is common along our roads and on neglected land.  It is a most undesirable weed in our nature reserves.
CONTROL: Because it is a monocotyledon (commonly referred to as a monocot) it cannot be controlled with the usual selective herbicides.  TARGET spray with Glyphosate.
ORIGIN: Indigenous to North Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Pentanisia: penta = five, anisos = unequal (the calyx lobes).
angustifolia: narrow leaf.
fields.Description:
A small perennial herb ±250-450 mm tall.
The plant regrows each spring.  
Its leaves are long and narrow and they often have very small hairs on the margins.
The flowers are in a dense terminal head, five-petalled and blue to violet-blue.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, north-eastern Free State and the eastern part of Eastern Cape.
Also in southern Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Pentarrhinum: penta = five, rhynchos = snout (shape of the corona).
insipidum: without taste.
fields.Description:
A slender, fast-growing, branching perennial vine up to 2 metres.  It winds itself around other plants or spreads along the ground.  It has a milky sap.  
The leaves are opposite, untoothed and heart-shaped.
The flower heads are carried in the axils of the leaves, the petals are purplish brown to greenish yellow. 
The flowers are produced in mid to late summer.  They have a yellow corona (a ring of structures attached to the corolla, i.e. the petals).
The fruit is an inflated follicle (a fruit that splits along a single seam – unlike a pod) ±60 x 15 mm, with a warty surface.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in all the provinces of South Africa and in much of Africa

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Pollichia: not known
campestris: of the fields or plains
fields.Description:
A small, much-branched, sprawling shrublet.
Leaves 4-8 x 2-5 mm, pointed at the tip. 
Densely clustered flower heads.  Tiny, white petals surrounded by white bracts.  
These develop around the seed-like fruits and are white or orange and fleshy.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Widespread in the eastern provinces of South Africa but also occurring in the Northern Cape and Western Cape.
Its range extends to Ethiopia.

fields.Common Names: Does not have a widely recognized, standardized English common name, but it belongs to a group of plants frequently referred to generally as Ironweeds
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Polydora: possibly named after Polydora, one of the Oceanides of the Ancient Greek mythology, minor goddesses and water nymphs of rivers, fountains etc.
poskeana: uncertain.
fields.Description:
An upright annual herb, branched or unbranched. 
The leaves are long and narrow 40-80 mm x 3-5 mm with the leaf margins rolled under, roughly but sparsely hairy.
The flower heads are spaced widely on long slender stems. What we would call the flower is in fact a composite flower head.  It is quite long and it has no ray florets, only disc florets.  These are purple.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Rietvlei, Kruin Park and probably other reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, Free State and Northern Cape.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Polygala: from Ancient Greek, = much milk, (the plant was thought to increase milk yields in cattle).
amatymbica: of the Thembu people. (Nelson Mandela was from the Thembu people).
fields.Description:
A small, prostrate, herbaceous perennial, ±80-140 mm high.
Its leaves have a very short leaf stem, are ±12 x 6 mm and they have a sharp point.
The purple flowers are borne between the leaves, solitary or in few-flowered clusters, in spring or early summer.  They have 2 enlarged petals and a fringed keel.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.   Also occurs in Lesotho and Swaziland.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Portulacaria:  suggests similarity to the common garden annual, Portulaca. 
afra: tells us that the plant occurs in Africa.
fields.Description:
An attractive, evergreen succulent shrub or small tree that grows to ± 2 metres in gardens.  It is smaller in Kruin Park.
Its stems are often reddish brown and its leaves are small round and fleshy.
Flowering in gardens is erratic and it has not flowered in Kruin Park but in its natural setting it is covered with masses of small, star-shaped pink in late winter and spring.
The Spekboom has been shown to be particularly effective in its ability to absorb carbon dioxide during photosynthesis, to convert it into plant tissue and oxygen and to release the oxygen back into the atmosphere.
fields.Notes:
INTRODUCED to Kruin Park. 
NOT native to the Pretoria area.  
Indigenous to the succulent Karoo scrub, dry river valleys, Savannah and thicket of Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.  Common in Addo Elephant National Park.
Also native to Swaziland and Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Priva: possibly from the old Gallic word briva meaning thoroughfare, but this is not certain.
fields.Description:
A soft sub-shrub, covered with coarse hairs.
The leaf stems are ±3-4 mm long and the leaves ±10x12 mm and have rounded teeth.  They are wide at the base and taper to the apex.  
The inflorescence (flower stem) is a long spike, the calyx is green and slightly ribbed and the 5-petalled, trumpet-shaped flowers are ±3-4mm long and wide, white with purple markings.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria. 
Indigenous to North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape.  Also in Botswana.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Protea: Proteus a Greek sea-god  who could change into many different shapes. (The name refers to the great diversity within the genus). 
caffra: from an old name for the eastern and central regions of South Africa, Kaffraria, where the type specimen plant was found.
fields.Description:
A small tree with an uneven, somewhat rounded, spreading crown. 
The bark is thick and dark brown with net-like fissures when mature. 
The leathery, grey-green leaves are elongated with nearly parallel sides. They are leathery in texture ±80-150 x 15-25mm.
What appears to be a flower is a flower head up to 80 mm in diameter with pink to reddish and sometimes creamy petal-like outer bracts (resembling petals) and many single creamy to pink flowers clustered together. 
The pollinated flower forms a small nut covered in reddish-brown hairs.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the southern slopes of Kruin Park and other Pretoria reserves, where the soil is quartzitic.
Occurs in Limpopo, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, parts of KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape as far south as the Katberg mountains.  It is also indigenous to Lesotho, a small part of eastern of Zimbabwe and western Mozambique

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Pseudo: false (not the same as).
gnaphalium: from gnaphalion, a Greek name for a downy plant.
oligandrum: oligo = small, andrum = anthers or stamens.
fields.Description:
An annual herb 400mm to 1 metre high, its stems are upright, single or branching near the base.  The stems are covered with white felt. 
The leaves are long and narrow ±25-60 × 4-8 mm, hairless and green above and white and felty beneath; the margins are curled under and usually wavy. 
The flower head at the apex of the stem is dense cluster. Each individual “flower” consists of a number of rows of shiny white membranous bracts.  The disk florets are yellowish. 
The fruit is small dry seed with a tuft of numerous soft bristles.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs mainly in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal, but also in Free State, Northern Cape, and the eastern parts of Eastern Cape.  
It is also indigenous to much of the southern and eastern parts of Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Psydrax: Wikipedia reports that this is from the Greek meaning a blister.  I can't find confirmation of this.
fields.Description:
A deciduous or semi-evergreen shrub or small tree, 2 metres high in Kruin Park.
The branches are opposite and tend to be horizontal. Young branches are green while the older branches are smooth and light grey.
The leaves are in opposite pairs, bright green above, dull below, and with prominent veins.
The ±3 mm flowers are creamy to yellow with green edges; they occur in clusters in the axils of the leaves in summer and they have an unpleasant odour.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.
Not endemic to South Africa, indigenous to Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Mozambique, Kenya and Angola.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Raphionacme: raphio (possibly from the Greek), meaning 'a needle' and acme, meaning a ‘point’, possibly a reference to the shape of the fruit.
galpinii: in honour of Ernest Galpin, a famous South African amateur botanist and plant collector.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb growing from an underground rootstock.
The flower buds are hairy. The tiny flowers open in October; they have five oblong green petals and a purplish centre above which there is a crown-like ring of spines that join at the top. 
The leaves are variable in shape ±70 mm long and ±10x12 mm wide. They are downy and have a pale midrib. 
By February, the fruit has developed into a cigar-like follicle, ±100-120 mm long and ±6-10 mm wide, tapering into a long point and covered with minute soft erect hairs.  It splits along one side to release the seed.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, and Eastern Cape.  
It also occurs further north in Africa.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Rhynchosia: from the Greek, rhynchos, meaning 'a beak', referring to the keel of the flowers.
adenodes: meaning 'with glandular knots'
fields.Description:
A prostrate herbaceous perennial, with a long, trailing stem, growing from a woody rootstock.
The stems may be smooth, or downy and covered with short, soft hairs.
The light green leaves are trifoliate, and the leaflets are egg-shaped to roundish and slightly downy. 
The inflorescence is 40–140 mm long and the flowers are about 10 mm across, yellow with orange or maroon veins on the petals. 
The fruit is a small pod, 15–18 × 4–6 mm, glabrous or glandular pubescent.
Flowering time is in spring, summer and autumn (September–June).
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
It occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, and Northern, Eastern and Western Cape.  Also in Lesotho.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Rhynchosia: from the Greek, rhynchos, meaning 'a beak', referring to the keel of the flowers.
nitens: glossy, shiny.
fields.Description:
An erect, sub-shrub, 50-80mm tall, densely covered with minute silky-silvery hairs. 
The leaves are on short leaf stems and have three ± 20-30 x ± 10-15 mm leaflets with the veins visible underneath.
The short flower stems carry 2 or 3 flowers.  The yellow flowers have 5 petals, a broad, upright petal (the standard), two short side petals (wings) and two petals fused at the tip and free at the base (the keel).
The fruit is a pod.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Northern Cape.
Also in Swaziland

fields.Family: Traditionally CAPRIFOLIACEAE, the Honeysuckle family.                In review, DIPSACACEAE, the Teasel family
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Scabiosa: from the Latin, it was believed to relieve the itch of scabies and skin sores.
columbaria: from the Latin meaning ‘a dove’, referring to some flower colour forms.
fields.Description:
An evergreen, perennial herb that grows up to 750 mm high, with branches developing from a woody rootstock. The light green, basal leaves are in a form of a rosette, with serrated or deeply lobed margins, slightly hairy on the upper surface.
The flowers are borne on multi-stemmed stalks up to 750 mm in height, with the flower heads about 25–35 mm in diameter.   Flowers are white or pink, appearing in spring and throughout summer.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to soem reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape and Northern Cape.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Scolopia: from the Greek, σκολοπες (skolopes) which is said to mean a thorn or pointed stick . 
zeyheri: in honour of K.L.P. Zeyher, a German botanist who was active in South Africa in the early 19th century.
fields.Description:
A tree, up to 4 or 5 metres in Kruin Park.  It tends to produce suckers (ie new shoots that originate from the roots some distance from the main stem of the plant).  It often has long spines on young trees and suckers but it is sparsely spiny on old trees.
The leaves have a short leaf stem and the blade of the leaf is ±2-8 x 1-3mm, very variable in shape, but generally more or less egg-shaped and often wider and rounded at the apex of the leaf, hairless, dark green above and paler on the reverse.
The flowers are in loose bunches in the leaf axils small, cream, fading to brown, in loose bunches at leaf axils.  The central mass of 3-4 mm stamens is prominent. They flower in winter.
The fruit is a small ±8 mm, round, reddish berry, tipped with the remains of the style. In late winter to early spring.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga highveld, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.
Also occurs in Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Searsia: named after Paul B. Sears, ecologist and head of the Yale School of Botany.
lancea: refers to the lance-shaped leaflets.
fields.Description:
A common evergreen tree (±4-6 metres tall in Kruin Park) usually branching quite close to the ground. 
The bark is coarse textured, reddish-brown on young branches and greyish brown on older branches.  
The compound leaves have three leaflets, and each leaflet is long (up to ±120 mm) and narrow.  The leaflets are a dull dark green and paler underneath. They are hairless, and untoothed.  Unlike Searsia leptodictya, the lateral leaflets are RARELY held at right angles to the terminal leaflet.
The inflorescence is a dense terminal spray of very small, pale greenish-yellow flowers.
The fruit is spherical often slightly asymmetrical, dull yellowish-brown and small (±4-5 mm).
fields.Notes:
UNCERTAIN whether Karee is truly indigenous to Kruin Park because its range in the reserve is limited to the area south of the reservoir where the material was imported at the time that the reservoir was developed.  Young trees are appearing in the grassland, so with the approval of the city’s Nature Conservation Division we were thinning these out to preserve the habitat of the short grassland wildflowers.
Indigenous to North West, Gauteng, much of Limpopo, the Mpumalanga Highveld, Free State, the western part of Northern Cape, and the drier parts of Eastern Cape and Western Cape.
Also occurs in Namibia, Botswana and Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Searsia: named after Paul B. Sears, ecologist
and head of the Yale School of Botany.
fields.Description:
A small tree up to 6 metres with an irregularly rounded crown and arching branches. It is evergreen in Pretoria but can be somewhat deciduous in cold areas and in cold winters.
The bark is rough and dark brown.
The leaves are divided into three narrow, bright green leaflets with toothed margins.  The lateral leaflets tend to be held at right angles to the terminal leaflet.
The tiny, yellowish flowers appear in sprays in mid to late summer. Male and female flowers occur on separate trees. 
The fruits are drupes (single-seeded stone fruit like a peach) ±5 mm across but flattened. In the autumn they go from greenish to yellowish to rusty brown.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, and Free State.  
Also in Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Searsia: named after Paul B. Sears, ecologist
and head of the Yale School of Botany.
magalismontanum: of the Magaliesberg.
fields.Description:
A dwarf, evergreen shrub, ±150-500 mm high and ±150 mm – 1 metre wide.
The young growth on the plant is often bronze, coral pink or red with numerous brownish dots, whereas the old stems are brown.
The leaves are trifoliate (with three leaflets), leathery and grey-green
The flowers are minute, creamy yellow and occur in dense sprays from October to November.
The fruit is yellowish, turning red when ripe from November to December and is slightly flattened.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and the Mpumalanga Highveld.
Also in Botswana.

fields.Common Names: Common Wild Currant, Taaibos, Motshakhutshakhu (Sepedi), Mogodiri (Setswana)
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Searsia: named after Paul B. Sears, ecologist and head of the Yale School of Botany.
pyroides: from the Greek ‘πυρός’ (pyros), meaning fire, referring to the painful sensation caused by a prick from the thorns.
fields.Description:
A small to medium-sized, deciduous tree, usually with several stems and with spines. 
The leaves have three leaflets. The leaflets are ±45-70 x 18-30 mm, oval, narrowing at both ends, and often with a round tip. They can be smooth or velvety above but the lower surface is usually slightly hairy. The midrib and the secondary veins are conspicuous.
The flowers are inconspicuous and greenish in bunches in the axils of the leaves and at the end of the branches.
The fruits are small and round, off-white turning red when they ripen in late summer.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs throughout the whole of South Africa.  Also indigenous to parts of Namibia and Botswana, Zimbabwe and Tanzania.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Searsia: named after Paul B. Sears, ecologist
and head of the Yale School of Botany.
zeyheri: in honour of K.L.P. Zeyher, a German botanist who was active in South Africa in the early 19th century.
fields.Description:
A small, deciduous shrub, ±1 metre tall.
The leaves are bluish-green and hairless. 
The tiny flowers are yellowish green and the fruits go from green to yellowish to red.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.
ENDEMIC to South Africa (i.e. it does not occur naturally elsewhere).

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Senecio: from the Latin senex which means old man.
oxyriifolius: means with leaves like the Alpine sorrel, Oxyria digyna.
fields.Description:
A fleshy, perennial herb.
The stem is erect, smooth and hairless, with leaves crowded towards the base. The pale grey-green, rounded leaves are on long stalks.  They are about 50–90 mm in diameter with small teeth and with pale veins. The flower stems are tall and slender, branched at the top and carry small yellow daisy flowers in spring and summer.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape.
Angola, DRC, Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Senecio: from the Latin senex which means old man.
venosus: the leaves are conspicuously veined.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb that produces stems from a rootstock in spring. 
It has bluish-green leaves, ±70 x 8 mm that clasp around the stem and have no leaf stem.
Held against the light, the leaves reveal clearly translucent veins.
The flower stems are tall and slender, branched at the top and carry small yellow daisy flowers in spring and summer.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and northern KwaZulu-Natal.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Senegalia: derived from the name of the country.
caffra: from the part of the Eastern Cape, called Caffraria by the early British colonists.
fields.Description:
A common deciduous tree, up to 6 metres in the shallow soils of Kruin Park, it has an irregular, spreading crown.  All the branches are armed with sharp hook thorns.  The trees tend to develop new branches from near the ground.
The leaves are arranged alternately on the stems and they are bipinnately compound (i.e. each leaf branches and then branches a second time).  
The new leaves and flowers appear at the same time in spring.  Initially the leaves are a fresh green.
Each pale yellow inflorescence (entire group of flowers) is a catkin consisting of many reddish-brown spherical buds that produce pale yellow filaments as they open.
The fruit is a pod that turns brown by late summer and which persists on the trees long after the leaves have fallen off.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape and Western Cape.
Also occurs beyond our borders.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Seriphium: said to be from serif, the small stroke or line of a letter (e.g. in PT Serif or Times Roman).
plumosum: meaning feathery.
fields.Description:
A sprawling shrub ±300 mm tall with very short internodes, and slender, ±10 mm x2 mm, woolly, grey-green leaves.
The white balls that look like cotton wool are not flowers; the flowers are brownish with purple tips.
This plant has become a troublesome weed on farms where the veld has been overgrazed. It certainly isn’t a troublesome plant in Kruin Park.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Widespread in all of South Africa and a common problem plant in pastures.
Also as far north as Angola, Zimbabwe and Mozambique

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Setaria: from the Latin seta meaning bristle or hair.
sphacelata: diseased, possibly referring to the appearance of the spike.
fields.Description:
A tufted perennial grass, ±600 - 1500 mm. 
The nodes (the usually thickened part of the stem where the leaves are attached) are hairless. 
The flower stem is a dense spike-like panicle, pink to pale-purplish with golden bristles 1.5-12 mm long.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape. 
Also in Botswana, Namibia, Malawi, Mozambique, Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Setaria: from the Latin seta meaning bristle or hair.
verticillata: from the Latin word meaning whorled
fields.Description:
A loosely tufted, sprawling, annual grass, from ±250–500 mm high.
The leaf blade is linear, ±50–200 × 6–12 mm, usually loosely hairy.
The inflorescence is spike-like, 20–70 mm long, armed with green bristles that are tinged purple, rigid, barbed and bent backwards, so that the inflorescences are often entangled.
fields.Notes:
NOT native to South Africa.
It is indigenous to Central and southern Europe and North Africa.  
It is a troublesome weed in our reserves.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Sphedamnocarpus: possibly from the Greek sfendamos a Maple and karpos fruit - referring to the winged fruits.
pruriens: causing itching.
fields.Description:
A slender, climbing plant with twining, hairy stems. 
The leaves are opposite or in whorls and are slightly hairy. 
The bright yellow flowers have five crinkly petals and they appear in summer.
The fruit is a samara (i.e. a winged fruit), generally with three hairy wings
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs mainly in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal but also in eastern Northern Cape.
Also occurs in Botswana, Namibia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Malawi.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Stapelia: named after Jan Bode van Stapel, a physician and botanist.
gigantea: huge, referring to the size of the flowers.
fields.Description:
A clump-forming, 4-sided succulent, with fleshy, upright stems and grooves between the angles. It grows ±200 mm high.
Dry rudimentary leaves are arranged along the angles.  
The 5-petalled, star-shaped flowers appear in late summer and autumn and are huge, ±200 mm across. They are brick red and yellow and fringed with long hairs.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the Pretoria area.
Occurs in the eastern parts of South Africa.
Also in Botswana, Zimbabwe, Swaziland, Mozambique, Malawi and Zambia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Striga: meaning a witch or a hag, probably because of the parasite’s negative impact on crops.
bilabiata: two-lipped.
fields.Description:
An erect, root parasite of grasses, it is an annual herb, 100-200 mm tall in Kruin Park.
The stems are usually unbranched, slightly hairy with whitish hairs. 
The narrow leaves are in opposite pairs, ±5-20 mm long, with rough, thick-based hairs. 
The flowers appear in late summer and are in dense terminal spikes, with several flowers open at the same time. 
The calyx tube is 2-3 mm long; with distinct 5-veined lobes. The flower has a tube up to 11 mm long ending in two pink, violet and sometimes whitish lips.
The fruit is a capsule ± 3 mm long and 1.5 mm wide.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.  It is a root parasite of grasses. 
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape
Also Namibia, Botswana, Lesotho, Swaziland, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Angola, DRC and Malawi.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms: Strychnos: from Ancient Greek 'στρύχνος' ('strúkhnos') .The plant, Strychnos nux-vomica, from southern Asia is the primary source of strychnine.
fields.Description:
A small tree that is generally evergreen here. 
The bark is grey to brown, smooth on young branches and rough on the main stem and older branches. 
The leaves are hairless, in opposite pairs 30-70 mm x 15-30 mm, rigid and they have a sharp point.
The greenish flowers are in small clusters at the axils of the leaves.
The hard, large fruit is up to 120 mm in diameter, green turning yellow when ripe.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs mainly in southern Limpopo, eastern North West, Gauteng and the Mpumalanga highveld with scattered populations further in Limpopo,
Also in Namibia, Botswana and Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Talinum: Uncertain.
caffrum: from an old name for the eastern and central regions of South Africa, Kaffraria.
fields.Description:
A fleshy perennial herb, up to 200 mm tall in Kruin Park.
It grows from a swollen tuber-like root. 
The leaves are ± 50 × 15 mm, and the margins are rolled under. 
The ±20 mm yellow flowers open in the afternoon and fade by nightfall. 
The fruit a roundish capsule.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
There are four species of Talinum that are very difficult to tell apart.  The species present in Kruin Park is Talinum caffrum.
Occurs in all of South Africa except the Western Cape.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Tephrosia: from the Greek 'τεφρος' (tephros), meaning "ash-colored," referring to the greyish leaves.
elongata: long in relation to the width, referring to the leaves.
fields.Description:
A slender perennial that grows from a woody rootstock.
The leaves are divided into three narrow leaflets ±100 x 10 mm.  Each leaflet has a main vein and numerous side veins and at the edges of the leaflets one can see the hairs protruding from the back.
The orange flowers are hairy on the reverse and are carried on thin flower stems.
The pods are also hairy.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.
Also further north to Malawi and Tanzania.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Tephrosia: from the Greek 'τεφρος' (tephros), meaning "ash-colored," referring to the greyish leaves.
longipes: from the Latin 'longus', (long) and 'pes' (foot), referring to the long flower stalks.
fields.Description:
A small, perennial herb, that grows from a woody rootstock. The leaves are divided into three narrow leaflets ±80 x 10 mm.
The flowers are on long stems and are pink, with rusty hairs on the standard (the top petal).
The fruit is a slender flat pod, covered with rusty hairs, especially along the margins.
fields.Notes: NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria and the Magaliesberg.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Teucrium: Possibly from the Greek name Teucer, a king of Troy.
trifidum: from the Latin word meaning three-cleft, referring to the leaf shape.
fields.Description:
A soft, upright sub-shrub, branching from the base.
The leaves are in opposite pairs, have three deep clefts, margins tending to curl under and are grey-green.
The flowers are white, tubular with 4 short lobes and one longer lobe.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape and the eastern part of Western Cape.
Also occurs in Botswana.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Thesium: possibly named after the legendary Greek hero Thesius.
utile: from the Latin 'utilis' (useful).
fields.Description:
A hemiparasite, i.e. a parasitic plant but having green leaves and stems, it is able to photosynthesize as opposed to a holoparasitic plant that is totally dependent on the host plant.
An upright plant with many stiff, erect stems that grows to ±300-450 mm high.  The stems are hairless, strongly ribbed and furrowed. 
The leaves are tiny and inconspicuous.
The five-petalled flowers are white, ±5 mm across and hairy on the inside.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng and Mpumalanga.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Tolpis: uncertain
capensis: from southern Africa (literally from the Cape).
fields.Description:
A perennial herb with its leaves in a basal rosette.
The leaves are slightly hairy, narrower at the base, with widely spaced wavy indentations.
Between a few and many flower heads are held on stems of about 200-300 mm and each “flower” has numerous ray florets.
fields.Notes:
Not clear whether it is native to Kruin Park or introduced with the soil brought in to form the platform around the reservoir.  
It occurs in all of South Africa but is commonest in the eastern provinces. It favours moister conditions.
Also in Africa as far north as Sudan.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Turbina: from the Latin ‘turbo’ or ‘turbinis’, (a whirlwind or cyclone).
oblongata: Latin, meaning oblong.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb that produces prostrate stems from a woody rootstock. 
The leaves are very variable in size and shape, usually oblong or elliptic, ±20-100 x 10-60 mm.  The margins and both surfaces of the leaf are usually hairy.

It has many flowers but they are short-lived.  They are funnel-shaped, 35-60 mm and bright magenta.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Rietvlei and Colbyn Valley.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape.
Also native to Lesotho. Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Swaziland and Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ursinia: in honour of Johann Heinrich Ursinus of Regensburg, a German cleric, theologian and botanist.
nana: small.
fields.Description:
An annual ± 200 mm high and about as wide. 
The leaves are feathery and divided irregularly into narrow segments.
The flower heads are carried on long leafless stems and the tip is drooping until the bud opens into a typical daisy with yellow ray-florets and yellow disk florets. 
Each seed has the usual “parachute-like” structure but instead of hairs it has two rows of white, petal-like scales and 5 bristles at the tip. August-October.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Rietvlei, Kruin Park and other Pretoria reserves.
Occurs in all of South Africa.
Also in Namibia.

fields.Family: FABACEAE, the bean family. Subfamily, Mimosoideae
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Vachellia: after Rev. George Harvey Vachell, a plant collector in China.
karroo: an old spelling of Karoo.
fields.Description:
A deciduous tree of ±2-6 metres in Kruin Park.
The bark of the young branches is reddish-brown, but it is darker and rougher on old branches. 
The bipinnately compound leaves are usually ±80 mm long, with 2-4 pairs of pinnae (secondary leaf segments) usually with ±8 dark green leaflets per pinna.
The flowers are sweet-smelling, spherical, bright yellow and ±15mm in diameter.
The fruit is a pod (like a bean).  Seedpods are sickle-shaped, initially green but turning reddish brown.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Rietvlei, Faerie Glen, Kruin Park and other reserves in Pretoria.
Occurs in all of South Africa except the winter rainfall part of Western Cape.  Its range extends further north to Angola and Zambia.

fields.Scientific Name: Vachellia robusta subsp. robusta, previously Acacia robusta subsp. robusta
fields.Family: FABACEAE, the bean family. Subfamily, Mimosoideae
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Vachellia: after Rev. George Harvey Vachell, a plant collector in China.
robusta: from the Latin robustus meaning strong.
fields.Description:
A fine deciduous tree ±4-5 metres tall and 7-8 metres wide in Kruin Park.  It has a dark brown deeply fissured trunk.
The spherical flowers are pale yellow and the pods are ±80-100 x20 x5 mm.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Northern Cape and Eastern Cape.

fields.Scientific Name: Vachellia tortilis subsp. heteracantha, previously Acacia tortilis subsp. heteracantha
fields.Family: FABACEAE, the bean family. Subfamily, Mimosoideae
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Vachellia: after Rev. George Harvey Vachell, a plant collector in China.
tortilis: twisted, a reference to the shape of the pods.
heteracantha: hetero (differing or variable) and 'ákanthos' (thorn).
fields.Description:
A slow-growing, deciduous, small to medium tree of between 5 and 8 metres. 
The bark on the trunk is rough and varies from medium grey to almost black, with somewhat tortuous longitudinal fissures. 
Young branches vary from olive green to brown or purplish. Older thicker branches are usually dark grey with some blackened fissures. 
As the name suggests the tree has straight and hooked thorns.  They are in pairs at the nodes.
Like all Vachellias, the flowers are spherical.  They are pale creamy yellow.
The fruit is a spiralled pod, like a coil spring.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Occurs in Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Northern Cape.
Also native to Zimbabwe.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Vangueria: from the Madagascan name for Vangueria edulis, voa vanguer. 
infausta: from the Latin (unlucky), referring to the magical properties it is believed to have.
fields.Description:
A small deciduous tree ±2-3 metres in Kruin Park, often with more than one main stem.
The light green leaves are ±100 x50 mm, in opposite pairs and are covered with short velvety hairs.
The flowers are ±5 mm and green and the ±25-35 mm fruits are green turning light brown.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Northern Cape and Eastern Cape.
Occurs further north as far as Tanzania.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Vernonia: named after the English botanist, William Vernon. 
galpinii: named after Ernest Galpin, banker and amateur botanist who collected the type specimen (the original, first described specimen) near Barberton in Mpumalanga.
fields.Description:
An upright perennial herb that grows each spring from a woody rootstock.
The leaves are in opposite pairs, have no leaf stem and are ±60 x 15 mm tapering to a point.
The ±25 mm flower heads are magenta-coloured, terminal and in the axils of the upper leaves.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to the reserves of Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape and Western Cape.
Occurs in Botswana, Zimbabwe, Swaziland and Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Vigna: from the Latin for a vine.
vexillata: means with a flag or standard
fields.Description:
A perennial climbing or trailing herb, that grows from a woody rootstock. Its stems are hairy.
It has three-lobed compound leaves, and the leaflets are ±25-120 mm long.  They may be hairless or velvety.
The flowers are typical for a plant in the bean family except that the lower boat-shaped keel is asymmetrical and twisted to the right.  They are pink to purple and appear in spring.  
The pods are 60-120 mm long and covered in brown bristly hairs.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to Colbyn Valley and probably other reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Eastern Cape.
Also native to Africa as far north as Nigeria and Ethiopia.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Viscum: from the Latin name for the plant, referring to the sticky birdlime made from the berries.
rotundifolium: round leaves.
fields.Description:
A hemiparasite, (i.e. a parasitic plant but having green leaves and stems, it is able to photosynthesize as opposed to a holoparasitic plant that is totally dependent on the host plant).
A small shrub with ribbed stems.
The leaves are in opposite pairs with no leaf stem.
The flowers are creamy-green, small and easily missed but the fruit is a bright orange or red berry.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to all of South Africa except the winter rainfall part of the Western Cape.
Also occurs in Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe and Angola.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Wahlenbergia: Named in honour of Georg Wahlenberg, a Swedish botanist.
undulata: undulate or wavy, referring to the leaf margins, which are always wavy.
fields.Description:
A perennial herb with long slender stems.
The leaves are mainly on the lower part of the stem (but not in a rosette).  They are long and narrow, and with untoothed margins and they have no leaf stem.
The jacaranda blue, bell-shaped flowers have 5 pointed lobes, and prominent 3-lobed styles. 
The 5 long pointed tips of the calyx remain around the ripening seed capsules. The seeds are released through 3 pores at the top of the seed capsule.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to many reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to all of South Africa.
Also further north as far as Tanzania.

fields.Scientific Name: Xerophyta retinervis, previously incorrectly, known as Vellozia retinervis
fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Xerophyta: from the Greek 'xeros' (dry) and 'phyton' (plant).
retinervis: (with a network of veins).
fields.Description:
A deciduous perennial with thick stems densely covered with closely packed fibres, often blackened by fire.
The long, strap-shaped leaves are carried at the top of the stems.
The flowers appear in spring and are pinkish-mauve on long thin stems. There is a white form. 
The fruit is a bristly capsule (a dry fruit which splits open to release the seeds).
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some reserves of Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Zanthoxylum: from the Greek 'xanthos' (yellow), and 'xylon' (wood).
capense: from southern Africa (literally from the Cape).
fields.Description:
A small tree ±4-5 metres in Kruin Park but taller in more favourable conditions.
The young stems have scattered thorns that become cone-shaped knobs on the main trunk and old branches.
The dark-green compound leaves have from 6 to many leaflets.
The tiny flowers are greenish-white and they have 4 sepals and 4 petals.
The fruit is a capsule (a dry fruit which splits open to release the seeds) that turns red and then splits to reveal a single black seed.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to some of Pretoria's reserves.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Eastern Cape and Western Cape.
Also in Zimbabwe and Mozambique.

fields.Meaning of Scientific name and synonyms:
Ziziphus: The ancient Greeks called the tree 'zizyphon', from the Arabic 'zizouf', a name for the mythical lotus.
mucronata: from mucronate meaning with a sharp, short point. The specimens in Kruin Park don't have a pointed leaf.
fields.Description:
A deciduous tree ±4-6 metres tall in Kruin Park.
The bark is rough with long, roughly rectangular blocks and it is dark reddish-brown to grey.
The leaves are shiny dark green, they have three veins branching from an asymmetrical base and very finely serrated edges.
The small flowers appear at the axils of the leaves and are yellowish-green.
The fruit is a drupe (with a single seed like a peach), ±12-20 mm, with dry flesh.  It is green turning brown when ripe.
fields.Notes:
NATIVE to several reserves in Pretoria.
Indigenous to Limpopo, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State, Northern Cape and Eastern Cape.
Also in Sub-Saharan Africa.
